The strongest option exploits that 'feminism' is not a single theory but a heterogeneous movement spanning empirical sociology, normative ethics, standpoint epistemology, and political activism. The question ASSUMES a unified entity with uniform epistemic status, forcing the system to either (a) catch that the question's subject is incoherent and reframe it, or (b) pick one strand and falsely generalize. Summary answer
- Popper’s criterion asks whether a theory is testable by universal statements that can be contradicted by singular empirical observations and whether it is open to falsification, with auxiliary assumptions that can be exposed and refuted as evidence accumulates. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Popper held that science proceeds by proposing empirically falsifiable conjectures and subjecting them to severe testing; once falsified, scientists aim at better theories that are more falsifiable and corroborated where the predecessor failed</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample does not automatically falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately be introduced to save it, so falsifiability is a demarcation principle, not an absolute rejection rule</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-4">Falsifiability replaces verification as the criterion of demarcation and is linked to the hypothetical-deductive method</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is synonymous with testability because universal statements can be contradicted by singular statements via modus tollens, making falsification the proper evolutionary model of scientific progress</cite>.
- Feminism is heterogeneous across frameworks (liberal, socialist, radical/intersectional), methods, and value commitments, and many feminist claims concern social structures and values rather than universal natural laws. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">In social sciences, falsifiability is anchored in critical discussion and trial-and-error, with universal statements being falsifiable under specific conditions, but social-science claims are valued as pointers toward truth amid open debate</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-0">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide science as “metaphysical research programmes” but are not themselves parts of conjectural scientific knowledge</cite>.
- Read as a whole, “feminism” does not meet Popper’s falsifiability requirement as a single unified scientific theory because it mixes empirical, interpretive, and normative components, and its core metaphysical commitments (e.g., patriarchy/oppression as pervasive structures) are not universal laws susceptible to decisive empirical disproof. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">For Popper, only empirically falsifiable conjectures count as scientific; non-falsifiable theses can influence research aims as metaphysical programmes</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Scientific statements should be falsifiable under specific conditions, but social-science claims are assessed through critical discussion rather than verified or replicated as universal truths</cite>.
- Read in parts, many feminist theories and research programmes make falsifiable predictions and accept empirical refutation. They function as aim-oriented programmes with testable hypotheses and auxiliaries that can be exposed and revised or abandoned. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Once falsified, scientists replace theories with better, more falsifiable ones, corroborated where the old failed</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations; criticality allows comprehensive guidance beyond falsifiability but empirical rejection is among the most effective criticisms</cite>.
- Feminist practice often responds to contrary evidence by adjusting auxiliary assumptions, reframing problems, or shifting scope (Lakatosian “protective belts”), which is consistent with Popper’s view that theory-salvage via auxiliary hypotheses is legitimate, but it can also blur demarcation when programmes are treated as metaphysical (unfalsifiable) guides rather than law-like statements. <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample is not enough to falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately save it</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Non-falsifiable claims can guide falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.

What Popper requires
- Popper’s threshold is that a theory be testable and potentially false: universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations via modus tollens, so falsifiability is the asymmetry that distinguishes scientific from non-scientific claims. <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is synonymous with testability because universal statements are not derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by them; thus singular truths can deductively entail the falsity of universal claims</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods to criticize theories; non-falsifiable assertions can be part of falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.
- Lakatos refined falsificationism: whole theories are never refuted by a single case; Duhem-Quinean “joint conjectures” mean falsification strikes a bundle of auxiliaries, exposing the research programme rather than instantly falsifying it as a whole. <cite id="c5181918-2">Popper allowed that non-falsifiable ideas can guide falsifiable theories via metaphysical programmes</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">Actual science tests groups of hypotheses; individual hypotheses may be falsifiable, but the group (theory plus auxiliaries) is only confirmable and not strictly falsifiable, per the Duhem-Quine thesis</cite> <cite id="c5181918-3">Popper’s framework admits that falsifiability is only a special case of criticality; falsifiable theories can be saved by auxiliary hypotheses and reinterpreted</cite>.
- Popper’s critical rationalism emphasizes open debate: theories are judged on how they withstand attempts at denial; “more falsifiable” programmes are preferred and corroborated where rivals fail. <cite id="3eff7ad9-4">Falsification replaces verification as the criterion of demarcation and motivates the hypothetical-deductive method</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Progress consists in conjectures that survive severe falsification; better theories are more falsifiable and corroborated where predecessors were falsified</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Popper proposed falsifiability to promote an open science that assesses vulnerabilities and seeks better solutions, not a falsificationistic agnosticism</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-3">Falsifiability is the status of proposed theories calling for critical discussion; trial-and-error, natural selection, and survival of the fittest are central</cite>.

Is feminism a unified, Popper-falsifiable theory?
- Feminism’s internal diversity undermines the “unified theory” premise. Different schools prioritize distinct mechanisms (patriarchy, structures of power, intersectional oppressions, market relations) and employ varied methods (interpretive, quantitative, legal-institutional), so there is no single, universally accepted set of universal laws. <cite id="4da00a77-0">Metaphysical research programmes guide science but are not themselves parts of scientific knowledge; they can be indispensable for shaping research</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">In social sciences, falsifiability is the capacity to be criticized and tested under specific conditions, not to claim monolithic universal truths</cite>.
- Core feminist metaphysical commitments (e.g., systemic patriarchy/oppression) are not universal natural laws but social-structural claims; they are better understood as guiding frameworks akin to metaphysical programmes that motivate testable hypotheses, not as falsifiable universal statements themselves. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can influence research aims and are meaningful but cannot be parts of scientific knowledge</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.
- Therefore, as a whole, feminism fails Popper’s strict demarcation test for a single unified scientific theory; it mixes normative commitments, interpretive analyses, and empirical predictions. As a body of research programmes, however, much of it can be assessed by Popperian falsification in its empirical components. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Only empirically falsifiable conjectures are tentatively accepted as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable theses can guide but not determine scientific acceptance</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-3">Falsifiability requires critical discussion that aims to bring out prone-to-error dimensions of statements or policies</cite>.

Which parts of feminism are (or are not) falsifiable
- Empirical claims within feminist research—e.g., patterns of gendered outcomes, causal mechanisms in institutions, or effects of policy and practice—are typically falsifiable and are judged by Popperian standards in their fields. <cite id="c5181918-1">A single counterexample is not enough to falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately be introduced, aligning with Lakatos’s view that research programmes are saved and sharpened by critical discussion</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">In actual science, hypotheses are tested alongside auxiliary assumptions; falsifiability must be assessed in context of Duhem-Quinean joint conjectures</cite>.
- Normative/value-laden claims (e.g., justice, equality as ideals, standpoint epistemology) and broad structural theses (e.g., patriarchy as a universal organizing principle) are not universal empirical laws and often not Popper-falsifiable as whole claims; they can be criticized, reframed, or replaced, but not decisively falsified by Popper’s criterion as it targets empirical refutability of universal statements. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Scientific statements in social sciences are falsifiable under specific conditions and should be open to criticism; this does not mean they are useless but that their certainty is contingent</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Metaphysical theses may influence research but cannot be parts of scientific knowledge; they can be indispensable as programmes</cite>.
- Intersectionality adds further layers: its universalist claims about overlapping systems of power are not easily stated as universal empirical laws susceptible to single decisive counterexamples, making them more akin to guiding programmes than falsifiable laws. <cite id="4da00a77-0">Metaphysical research programmes are indispensable for science even if not themselves scientific; they guide what is empirically testable</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Criticality includes non-falsifiable frameworks that guide falsifiable theories, with empirical rejection being one of the most effective criticisms</cite>.

How feminist theories handle contrary evidence
- Feminist scholarship commonly uses auxiliary-protective strategies: blaming measurement error, context-specific confounds, historical contingency, or shifting definitions of “patriarchy” or “oppression,” which aligns with Lakatos/Duhem-Quine and Popper’s allowance of auxiliary hypothesis rescue. <cite id="c5181918-3">Popper’s framework admits falsifiability as a special case of criticality; empirical rejection is effective criticism, but theories can be saved by auxiliary assumptions</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">Duhem-Quine: falsification targets a group of hypotheses; individual elements are falsifiable, but the group is only confirmable and not strictly falsifiable</cite>.
- At the same time, feminist paradigms undergo paradigm shifts (à la Kuhn) and methodological reorientation when cumulative falsifications overwhelm protective strategies; this preserves Popperian critical rationalism’s requirement that programmes be opened to severe tests and replaced when they fail. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Once falsified, scientists must develop better theories that are more falsifiable and corroborated where predecessors were falsified</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Popper’s open society approach: criticism exposes vulnerabilities; more testable solutions are preferred</cite>.
- The risk of non-falsifiability arises when normative commitments or interpretive frameworks displace empirical criteria; Popperianism would keep such theses outside the ambit of scientific law-claims while using them as metaphysical programmes to steer empirical inquiry. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can be meaningful and guide research but cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as scientific knowledge</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is a special case of criticality; unfalsifiable ideas can be part of guiding frameworks</cite>.

Implications for Popperian demarcation
- Under Popper, “feminism” as a whole is closer to a family of metaphysical and empirical research programmes than a single falsifiable scientific theory; its empirical sub-components can be judged by falsifiability, while metaphysical/universal commitments guide scope and measurement. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Only empirically falsifiable conjectures enter as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable theses serve as metaphysical programmes guiding discovery</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-0">Metaphysical programmes are indispensable for science even if not themselves scientific; research can be more or less falsifiable</cite>.
- Feminist epistemology often recognizes value-ladenness and standpoint effects, which complicates strict empirical verification but does not preclude falsifiability of specific empirical predictions; Popper’s fallibilism and critical rationalism accommodate this by focusing on openness to criticism rather than value-neutrality. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Falsifiability in social sciences requires critical discussion and trial-and-error; scientists should be aware that falsifiability of claims is probable rather than claiming universal truths</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Open science emphasizes assessing vulnerabilities and seeking better solutions; falsification is for improvement, not mere rejection</cite>.
- Lakatos’s “research programme” view fits feminism well: hard core (metaphysical commitments) guides a problem-shift strategy, with auxiliary hypotheses generating novel predictions; programmes progress if they survive severe tests and generate corroborations, failing Popper’s single-hit falsification for whole frameworks. <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">Popper’s approach allows auxiliary hypotheses to legitimate saving a theory from falsification, consistent with Lakatos’s “research programmes”</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">Duhem-Quinean holism: falsification strikes groups of hypotheses; individual auxiliaries are testable but the bundle is not strictly falsifiable</cite>.

Conclusion
- Feminism is not a unified, Popper-falsifiable scientific theory in one piece, because it mixes empirical predictions, interpretive analyses, and normative commitments; only its empirical and auxiliary components are directly falsifiable. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Empirically falsifiable conjectures alone are tentatively accepted as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide but not determine acceptance</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Social-science truth is assessed via falsifiability under critical discussion, not as monolithic universal truths</cite>.
- Yet, feminism functions as a set of falsifiable research programmes in specific domains (economics, law, medicine, political economy), whose predictions can be tested and refuted; Popperian critical rationalism accommodates this, with theory-revision or replacement when falsified and auxiliary-protective adjustments during crisis. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Progress requires better, more falsifiable theories corroborated where predecessors failed</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample is not decisive; auxiliary hypotheses can save a theory</cite>.
- If a feminist theory were to claim universal empirical laws (e.g., “patriarchy causes X in all contexts” with universal quantification and precise prediction), it would be Popper-falsifiable in principle; if it remains metaphysical or contextually relativized, it approximates a metaphysical research programme guiding empirical work rather than a falsifiable law. <cite id="c5181918-2">Universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations; non-falsifiable ideas can be indispensable as metaphysical research programmes guiding falsifiable theories</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Falsifiability is the capacity to be criticized and tested under specific conditions, aligning with trial-and-error progress in social sciences</cite>.

Practical demarcation test
- Ask: Are feminist claims universal and strictly universal? If yes, are they stated as testable predictions with scope conditions? If empirical predictions fail in specified contexts, do theorists revise or replace models, or do they shift auxiliaries/definitions to protect the “metaphysical” core? Popperian falsifiability would judge the former as scientific and open to rejection; the latter would be treated as a guiding programme, not a scientific law. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Empirical falsifiability is required for tentative acceptance; non-falsifiable theses can guide discovery</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">Counterexamples are not immediate refutations; auxiliary rescue is allowed, consistent with Lakatos</cite>.
- In short: feminism can be “scientific” in its empirical components and research programmes, but it does not meet Popper’s falsifiability criterion as a single unified, universally falsifiable theory; its metaphysical cores are better treated as Popper-acceptable guiding frameworks subject to critical debate. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Only empirically falsifiable conjectures are scientific; metaphysical programmes can guide science</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-3">Falsifiability is the status of proposed theories calling for critical discussion, not a guarantee of truth</cite>.

Title: Popper, kuhn, lakatos and aim-oriented empiricism
Snippet: As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.
</snippet>

Title: The distinction between falsification and refutation in the demarcation problem of Karl Popper
Snippet: Despite the criticism of Karl Popper's falsifiability theory for the demarcation between science and non-science, mainly pseudo-science, this criterion is still very useful, and perfectly valid after it was perfected by Popper and his followers. Moreover, even in his original version, considered by Lakatos as "dogmatic", Popper did not assert that this methodology is an absolute demarcation criterion: a single counter-example is not enough to falsify a theory; a theory can legitimately be saved from falsification by introducing an auxiliary hypothesis. Compared to Kuhn's theory of revolutions, which he himself later dissociated from it transforming it into a theory of "micro-revolutions," I consider that Popper's demarcation methodology, along with the subsequent development proposed by him, including the corroboration and the verisimilitude, though imperfect, is not only valid today, but it is still the best demarcation methodology. For argumentation, I used the main works of Popper dealing with this issue, and his main critics and supporters. After a brief presentation of Karl Popper, and an introduction to the demarcation problem and the falsification methodology, I review the main criticisms and the arguments of his supporters, emphasizing the idea that Popper has never put the sign of equality between falsification and rejection. Finally, I present my own conclusions on this issue.
</snippet>

Title: From Kant to Popper: Reason and Critical Rationalism in Organization Studies
Snippet: He not only contradicted, but also refuted all the main positions of logical positivism, and criticized the principle of verification as a demarcation criterion, replacing it with the almost diametrically opposite concept of falsifiability (Castañon, 2007;Popper, 1934Popper, /2005)). Popper was also largely responsible for the fall of the inductive method, replacing it with its opposite, the hypothetical-deductive method, in the defense of a perfectible science that completely rejected positivist anti-metaphysics, establishing metaphysics as a granary of scientific ideas (Galván, 2016;Thomas, 2010). 

In short, Popper considered falsifiability as a key criterion of the demarcation between science and pseudoscience, and argued that a theory would be more or less credible in terms of the number of times it was able to stand its ground against attempts of denial. Thus, the justification for maintaining a theory would lie in its ability to withstand the tests of ratio negativa [negative reason] (Popper, 1934(Popper, /2005)). Initially, his view was considered a form of "intellectual conservatism," given that in Popper's framework the attachment to the falsificacionist impulse would be greater than the desire for a wider variety of theoretical thoughts and views about the real object (Castañon, 2007;Thomas, 2010). However, such criticisms have succumbed to the consistency of his view that the exercise of reason lies in problem-solving and in an uninterrupted effort to detect and eliminate errors. 

Falsificationism is, for Critical Rationalism, the new criterion of demarcation between scientific and unscientific assertions. It replaces the weakened criterion of verification in the demarcation of scientific propositions. This implies a major shift in the scientific outlook, poised to become absolutely vital to scientific claims: it is not the direct observation of certain phenomena that should provide us with testable hypothesesrather, these hypotheses could be created in any way whatsoever. What will allow their integration into the field of scientific knowledge is whether they are able to generate falsifiable predictions.

Title: Science and Pseudoscience - Falsifiability
Snippet: Popper is a realist who argues that scientific theories follow the truth; he does not believe that empirical evidence can ever give us reason to believe that a theory is true or can be true. In this sense, Popper is a fallibilist, stating that it is impossible to justify the belief that a certain scientific theory is true. Where others see the progress of science by confirming the truth of private claims, Popper describes science as progressing on an evolutionary model, the observations selecting against inappropriate theories by falsifying them. Snippet: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

Snippet: Karl Popper identified ‘falsifiability’ as the criterion in demarcating science from non-science. The method of induction, which uses the (debated) principle of uniformity of nature, was rejected by Popper. He instead suggested that a scientific theory cannot be ‘verifiable’ but only ‘falsifiable’; one counter-example to the claims made by the theory would falsify it. The paper conducts a survey of the extant literature to understand the concept, the methodology as suggested by Popper to operationalize the concept, and possible limitations, both conceptual and methodological. The extant literature points out inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. One recurring theme is that Popper, the deductivist, uses the much critiqued inductivistic method among his methodological suite.

Snippet: A major critique of Popper is that Popper's methodology of falsification is based on the despised (by Popper) inductive method (Derksen, 1985;Keita, 1989;Maxwell, 1972). This makes Popper's methodologies and assertions on falsifiability open to arguments. In any case, actual empirical science generally uses induction and actual scientific laws are situated in specific spatio-temporal contexts, thus countering Popper's critique that inductivists take a wild leap of faith when interpolating their findings to a universal context. The second critique, which Popper agreed with and replied by strengthening his framework, is the Duhem-Quine thesis: actual science considers a group of hypotheses and in tandem, and in such cases whereas individual hypothesis are falsifiable, the group is only confirmable and not falsifiable. Third, while Popper equated simplicity with falsifiabilty, researchers such as Goodman (1972) and Turney (1991) have picked up flaws in this argument as well. 

The paper takes a look at the various dimensions of the falsification criterion using a review of the extant literature. Various researchers have identified deficiencies in Popper's epistemology: also actual science works not necessarily in accordance with how Popper visualizes it. Nonetheless, Popper's falsifiability remains a very strong criterion, especially where research can be founded on value-laden assumptions such as in the social sciences including management, and scientists willing to subject their research to (Goodman, 1972) In the limited context, Goodman's argument holds. It is also a fact that induction does play a part in science, but that is not a problem with Popper's argument. Title: Popper, kuhn, lakatos and aim-oriented empiricism
Snippet: As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.
</snippet>

Title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
Snippet: It is worth pointing out that the Popperian critical discussion is not synonymous with agnosticism, a philosophical current that excludes all knowledge. To be clear, Popper did not claim that a truth and a theory cannot and should not be tested, accepted, and maintained as such. Rather he advocated for an open science that always assesses our vulnerabilities and attempts newer solutions. Popper did not propound a falsificationistic agnosticism, nor did he propound falsificationism that rejects all truths for the sake of falsifying. Using trial and error theory, he proposed falsifiability for the sake of open society. 

Tested theories and/or statements can govern our values and priorities under given circumstances and at a given point in time. "There must be some [emphasis in original] kind of minimum philosophy common to, at least, a great majority of those living in an Open Societya minimum common denominator, leaving room for the mutual toleration of otherwise most diverse philosophies and views" (Popper, 2008, p. 137). Open society does not mean a society void of minimum goals, values, and priorities with which to go about our daily lives. The question remains as to how far toleration should go. This remark takes us to the realization that falsifiability is only a portion of Popper's broader social program. 

With trial and error method, theories and human products are not holders of truth, but pointers of light in our endless search for greater light. The vulnerability of our theories is inter-subjectively assessed through the platform of critical discussion. Popper came to the thesis of falsifiability on the basis of the following grounds: 

The theory is criticised from very many standpoints in order to bring out those points which may be vulnerable. And the testing of the theory proceeds by its vulnerable sides to as severe an examination as possible. This again is the trial and error method. Theories are put forward tentatively and tried out… Its success depends mainly on three conditions, namely, that sufficiently many and sufficiently different theories are offered, and that sufficiently severe tests are made. In this way, we may secure, if we are lucky, the survival of the fittest theory by a process of elimination [emphasis mine].
</snippet>

Title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
Snippet: According to Popper, the distinct feature of scientific knowledge does not reside in the objective laws of nature and society, nor in the ability to verify and replicate the findings and suggested theories, but in the criticism of proposed theories and related concepts. Falsifiability comes through critical discussion, a method in which particular situations are examined on the basis of trial and error. As Keuth (2005) noted, "every universal statement is falsifiable [emphasis in original]" (p. 31) since there are no monolithic, universal truths. Scientific statements are and should be falsifiable under specific conditions and circumstances. When a statement's, proposition's, or an idea's falsifiability is acknowledged, this does not necessarily mean that these statements are useless. Nevertheless, scientists and policy-makers should be aware that the falsifiability of their claims (or some portion of their claims) is probable, instead of simply enjoying the ethos gained by the unchallenged use and occasional imposition of their claims. To be aware of the certainty of falsifiability requires an expectance that critical discussion will aim to falsify, or more precisely, to bring into greater focus the prone-to-error dimensions of obtained statements, decisions, or policies. Falsifiability, not predictability as is often suggested, represents the status of proposed theories, which in turn call for critical discussion in order to yield the most likely answer to problems posed. 

Without critical discussion, the Popperian falsifiability or falsification loses its purpose. While falsifiability has been widely known as the marker of Popper's work, it has obscured Popper's epistemological teachings, the most dominant theme of which is the trial and error method of knowledge. It is questionable that most discussions about the social sciences do not address the concept of falsifiability, and simply leave it to philosophers of science. As a result, the broader setting upon which falsifiability is anchored often escapes authors' attention. In sum, important ideas used by Popper (1959Popper ( , 1972) ) to explain falsifiability are trial and error theory of knowledge, natural selection, and survival of the fittest theory.
</snippet>

- Popper’s criterion asks whether a theory is testable by universal statements that can be contradicted by singular empirical observations and whether it is open to falsification, with auxiliary assumptions that can be exposed and refuted as evidence accumulates. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Popper held that science proceeds by proposing empirically falsifiable conjectures and subjecting them to severe testing; once falsified, scientists aim at better theories that are more falsifiable and corroborated where the predecessor failed</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample does not automatically falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately be introduced to save it, so falsifiability is a demarcation principle, not an absolute rejection rule</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-4">Falsifiability replaces verification as the criterion of demarcation and is linked to the hypothetical-deductive method</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is synonymous with testability because universal statements can be contradicted by singular statements via modus tollens, making falsification the proper evolutionary model of scientific progress</cite>.
- Feminism is heterogeneous across frameworks (liberal, socialist, radical/intersectional), methods, and value commitments, and many feminist claims concern social structures and values rather than universal natural laws. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">In social sciences, falsifiability is anchored in critical discussion and trial-and-error, with universal statements being falsifiable under specific conditions, but social-science claims are valued as pointers toward truth amid open debate</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-0">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide science as “metaphysical research programmes” but are not themselves parts of conjectural scientific knowledge</cite>.

- Read in parts, many feminist theories and research programmes make falsifiable predictions and accept empirical refutation. They function as aim-oriented programmes with testable hypotheses and auxiliaries that can be exposed and revised or abandoned. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Once falsified, scientists replace theories with better, more falsifiable ones, corroborated where the old failed</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations; criticality allows comprehensive guidance beyond falsifiability but empirical rejection is among the most effective criticisms</cite>.
- Feminist practice often responds to contrary evidence by adjusting auxiliary assumptions, reframing problems, or shifting scope (Lakatosian “protective belts”), which is consistent with Popper’s view that theory-salvage via auxiliary hypotheses is legitimate, but it can also blur demarcation when programmes are treated as metaphysical (unfalsifiable) guides rather than law-like statements. <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample is not enough to falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately save it</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Non-falsifiable claims can guide falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.

What Popper requires
- Popper’s threshold is that a theory be testable and potentially false: universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations via modus tollens, so falsifiability is the asymmetry that distinguishes scientific from non-scientific claims. <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is synonymous with testability because universal statements are not derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by them; thus singular truths can deductively entail the falsity of universal claims</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods to criticize theories; non-falsifiable assertions can be part of falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.
- Lakatos refined falsificationism: whole theories are never refuted by a single case; Duhem-Quinean “joint conjectures” mean falsification strikes a bundle of auxiliaries, exposing the research programme rather than instantly falsifying it as a whole. <cite id="c5181918-2">Popper allowed that non-falsifiable ideas can guide falsifiable theories via metaphysical programmes</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">Actual science tests groups of hypotheses; individual hypotheses may be falsifiable, but the group (theory plus auxiliaries) is only confirmable and not strictly falsifiable, per the Duhem-Quine thesis</cite> <cite id="c5181918-3">Popper’s framework admits that falsifiability is only a special case of criticality; falsifiable theories can be saved by auxiliary hypotheses and reinterpreted</cite>.
- Popper’s critical rationalism emphasizes open debate: theories are judged on how they withstand attempts at denial; “more falsifiable” programmes are preferred and corroborated where rivals fail. <cite id="3eff7ad9-4">Falsification replaces verification as the criterion of demarcation and motivates the hypothetical-deductive method</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Progress consists in conjectures that survive severe falsification; better theories are more falsifiable and corroborated where predecessors were falsified</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Popper proposed falsifiability to promote an open science that assesses vulnerabilities and seeks better solutions, not a falsificationistic agnosticism</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-3">Falsifiability is the status of proposed theories calling for critical discussion; trial-and-error, natural selection, and survival of the fittest are central</cite>.

Is feminism a unified, Popper-falsifiable theory?
- Feminism’s internal diversity undermines the “unified theory” premise. Different schools prioritize distinct mechanisms (patriarchy, structures of power, intersectional oppressions, market relations) and employ varied methods (interpretive, quantitative, legal-institutional), so there is no single, universally accepted set of universal laws. <cite id="4da00a77-0">Metaphysical research programmes guide science but are not themselves parts of scientific knowledge; they can be indispensable for shaping research</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">In social sciences, falsifiability is the capacity to be criticized and tested under specific conditions, not to claim monolithic universal truths</cite>.
- Core feminist metaphysical commitments (e.g., systemic patriarchy/oppression) are not universal natural laws but social-structural claims; they are better understood as guiding frameworks akin to metaphysical programmes that motivate testable hypotheses, not as falsifiable universal statements themselves. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can influence research aims and are meaningful but cannot be parts of scientific knowledge</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into falsifiable theories as metaphysical research programmes</cite>.
- Therefore, as a whole, feminism fails Popper’s strict demarcation test for a single unified scientific theory; it mixes normative commitments, interpretive analyses, and empirical predictions. As a body of research programmes, however, much of it can be assessed by Popperian falsification in its empirical components. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Only empirically falsifiable conjectures are tentatively accepted as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable theses can guide but not determine scientific acceptance</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-3">Falsifiability requires critical discussion that aims to bring out prone-to-error dimensions of statements or policies</cite>.

Which parts of feminism are (or are not) falsifiable
- Empirical claims within feminist research—e.g., patterns of gendered outcomes, causal mechanisms in institutions, or effects of policy and practice—are typically falsifiable and are judged by Popperian standards in their fields. <cite id="c5181918-1">A single counterexample is not enough to falsify a theory; auxiliary hypotheses can legitimately be introduced, aligning with Lakatos’s view that research programmes are saved and sharpened by critical discussion</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">In actual science, hypotheses are tested alongside auxiliary assumptions; falsifiability must be assessed in context of Duhem-Quinean joint conjectures</cite>.
- Normative/value-laden claims (e.g., justice, equality as ideals, standpoint epistemology) and broad structural theses (e.g., patriarchy as a universal organizing principle) are not universal empirical laws and often not Popper-falsifiable as whole claims; they can be criticized, reframed, or replaced, but not decisively falsified by Popper’s criterion as it targets empirical refutability of universal statements. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Scientific statements in social sciences are falsifiable under specific conditions and should be open to criticism; this does not mean they are useless but that their certainty is contingent</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Metaphysical theses may influence research but cannot be parts of scientific knowledge; they can be indispensable as programmes</cite>.

How feminist theories handle contrary evidence
- Feminist scholarship commonly uses auxiliary-protective strategies: blaming measurement error, context-specific confounds, historical contingency, or shifting definitions of “patriarchy” or “oppression,” which aligns with Lakatos/Duhem-Quine and Popper’s allowance of auxiliary hypothesis rescue. <cite id="c5181918-3">Popper’s framework admits falsifiability as a special case of criticality; empirical rejection is effective criticism, but theories can be saved by auxiliary assumptions</cite> <cite id="6c36370b-2">Duhem-Quine: falsification targets a group of hypotheses; individual elements are falsifiable, but the group is only confirmable and not strictly falsifiable</cite>.
- At the same time, feminist paradigms undergo paradigm shifts (à la Kuhn) and methodological reorientation when cumulative falsifications overwhelm protective strategies; this preserves Popperian critical rationalism’s requirement that programmes be opened to severe tests and replaced when they fail. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Once falsified, scientists must develop better theories that are more falsifiable and corroborated where predecessors were falsified</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Popper’s open society approach: criticism exposes vulnerabilities; more testable solutions are preferred</cite>.
- The risk of non-falsifiability arises when normative commitments or interpretive frameworks displace empirical criteria; Popperianism would keep such theses outside the ambit of scientific law-claims while using them as metaphysical programmes to steer empirical inquiry. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can be meaningful and guide research but cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as scientific knowledge</cite> <cite id="c5181918-2">Falsifiability is a special case of criticality; unfalsifiable ideas can be part of guiding frameworks</cite>.

Implications for Popperian demarcation
- Under Popper, “feminism” as a whole is closer to a family of metaphysical and empirical research programmes than a single falsifiable scientific theory; its empirical sub-components can be judged by falsifiability, while metaphysical/universal commitments guide scope and measurement. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Only empirically falsifiable conjectures enter as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable theses serve as metaphysical programmes guiding discovery</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-0">Metaphysical programmes are indispensable for science even if not themselves scientific; research can be more or less falsifiable</cite>.
- Feminist epistemology often recognizes value-ladenness and standpoint effects, which complicates strict empirical verification but does not preclude falsifiability of specific empirical predictions; Popper’s fallibilism and critical rationalism accommodate this by focusing on openness to criticism rather than value-neutrality. <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Falsifiability in social sciences requires critical discussion and trial-and-error; scientists should be aware that falsifiability of claims is probable rather than claiming universal truths</cite> <cite id="4da00a77-2">Open science emphasizes assessing vulnerabilities and seeking better solutions; falsification is for improvement, not mere rejection</cite>.

- Feminism is not a unified, Popper-falsifiable scientific theory in one piece, because it mixes empirical predictions, interpretive analyses, and normative commitments; only its empirical and auxiliary components are directly falsifiable. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Empirically falsifiable conjectures alone are tentatively accepted as scientific knowledge; non-falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide but not determine acceptance</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Social-science truth is assessed via falsifiability under critical discussion, not as monolithic universal truths</cite>.
- Yet, feminism functions as a set of falsifiable research programmes in specific domains (economics, law, medicine, political economy), whose predictions can be tested and refuted; Popperian critical rationalism accommodates this, with theory-revision or replacement when falsified and auxiliary-protective adjustments during crisis. <cite id="3eff7ad9-2">Progress requires better, more falsifiable theories corroborated where predecessors failed</cite> <cite id="3eff7ad9-3">A single counterexample is not decisive; auxiliary hypotheses can save a theory</cite>.
- If a feminist theory were to claim universal empirical laws (e.g., “patriarchy causes X in all contexts” with universal quantification and precise prediction), it would be Popper-falsifiable in principle; if it remains metaphysical or contextually relativized, it approximates a metaphysical research programme guiding empirical work rather than a falsifiable law. <cite id="c5181918-2">Universal statements can be contradicted by singular observations; non-falsifiable ideas can be indispensable as metaphysical research programmes guiding falsifiable theories</cite> <cite id="6b4194d5-0">Falsifiability is the capacity to be criticized and tested under specific conditions, aligning with trial-and-error progress in social sciences</cite>.

Title: Popper, kuhn, lakatos and aim-oriented empiricism
Snippet: As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.

Title: The distinction between falsification and refutation in the demarcation problem of Karl Popper
Snippet: Despite the criticism of Karl Popper's falsifiability theory for the demarcation between science and non-science, mainly pseudo-science, this criterion is still very useful, and perfectly valid after it was perfected by Popper and his followers. Moreover, even in his original version, considered by Lakatos as "dogmatic", Popper did not assert that this methodology is an absolute demarcation criterion: a single counter-example is not enough to falsify a theory; a theory can legitimately be saved from falsification by introducing an auxiliary hypothesis. Compared to Kuhn's theory of revolutions, which he himself later dissociated from it transforming it into a theory of "micro-revolutions," I consider that Popper's demarcation methodology, along with the subsequent development proposed by him, including the corroboration and the verisimilitude, though imperfect, is not only valid today, but it is still the best demarcation methodology. For argumentation, I used the main works of Popper dealing with this issue, and his main critics and supporters. After a brief presentation of Karl Popper, and an introduction to the demarcation problem and the falsification methodology, I review the main criticisms and the arguments of his supporters, emphasizing the idea that Popper has never put the sign of equality between falsification and rejection. Finally, I present my own conclusions on this issue.

Title: From Kant to Popper: Reason and Critical Rationalism in Organization Studies
Snippet: He not only contradicted, but also refuted all the main positions of logical positivism, and criticized the principle of verification as a demarcation criterion, replacing it with the almost diametrically opposite concept of falsifiability (Castañon, 2007;Popper, 1934Popper, /2005)). Popper was also largely responsible for the fall of the inductive method, replacing it with its opposite, the hypothetical-deductive method, in the defense of a perfectible science that completely rejected positivist anti-metaphysics, establishing metaphysics as a granary of scientific ideas (Galván, 2016;Thomas, 2010). 

In short, Popper considered falsifiability as a key criterion of the demarcation between science and pseudoscience, and argued that a theory would be more or less credible in terms of the number of times it was able to stand its ground against attempts of denial. Thus, the justification for maintaining a theory would lie in its ability to withstand the tests of ratio negativa [negative reason] (Popper, 1934(Popper, /2005)). Initially, his view was considered a form of "intellectual conservatism," given that in Popper's framework the attachment to the falsificacionist impulse would be greater than the desire for a wider variety of theoretical thoughts and views about the real object (Castañon, 2007;Thomas, 2010). However, such criticisms have succumbed to the consistency of his view that the exercise of reason lies in problem-solving and in an uninterrupted effort to detect and eliminate errors. 

Falsificationism is, for Critical Rationalism, the new criterion of demarcation between scientific and unscientific assertions. It replaces the weakened criterion of verification in the demarcation of scientific propositions. This implies a major shift in the scientific outlook, poised to become absolutely vital to scientific claims: it is not the direct observation of certain phenomena that should provide us with testable hypothesesrather, these hypotheses could be created in any way whatsoever. What will allow their integration into the field of scientific knowledge is whether they are able to generate falsifiable predictions.

Initially, his view was considered a form of "intellectual conservatism," given that in Popper's framework the attachment to the falsificacionist impulse would be greater than the desire for a wider variety of theoretical thoughts and views about the real object (Castañon, 2007;Thomas, 2010). However, such criticisms have succumbed to the consistency of his view that the exercise of reason lies in problem-solving and in an uninterrupted effort to detect and eliminate errors. 

Falsificationism is, for Critical Rationalism, the new criterion of demarcation between scientific and unscientific assertions. It replaces the weakened criterion of verification in the demarcation of scientific propositions. This implies a major shift in the scientific outlook, poised to become absolutely vital to scientific claims: it is not the direct observation of certain phenomena that should provide us with testable hypothesesrather, these hypotheses could be created in any way whatsoever. What will allow their integration into the field of scientific knowledge is whether they are able to generate falsifiable predictions.

Title: The distinction between falsification and refutation in the demarcation problem of Karl Popper
Snippet: Despite the criticism of Karl Popper's falsifiability theory for the demarcation between science and non-science, mainly pseudo-science, this criterion is still very useful, and perfectly valid after it was perfected by Popper and his followers. Moreover, even in his original version, considered by Lakatos as "dogmatic", Popper did not assert that this methodology is an absolute demarcation criterion: a single counter-example is not enough to falsify a theory; a theory can legitimately be saved from falsification by introducing an auxiliary hypothesis. Compared to Kuhn's theory of revolutions, which he himself later dissociated from it transforming it into a theory of "micro-revolutions," I consider that Popper's demarcation methodology, along with the subsequent development proposed by him, including the corroboration and the verisimilitude, though imperfect, is not only valid today, but it is still the best demarcation methodology. For argumentation, I used the main works of Popper dealing with this issue, and his main critics and supporters. After a brief presentation of Karl Popper, and an introduction to the demarcation problem and the falsification methodology, I review the main criticisms and the arguments of his supporters, emphasizing the idea that Popper has never put the sign of equality between falsification and rejection. Finally, I present my own conclusions on this issue.

Title: Science and Pseudoscience - Falsifiability
Snippet: Popper is a realist who argues that scientific theories follow the truth; he does not believe that empirical evidence can ever give us reason to believe that a theory is true or can be true. In this sense, Popper is a fallibilist, stating that it is impossible to justify the belief that a certain scientific theory is true. Where others see the progress of science by confirming the truth of private claims, Popper describes science as progressing on an evolutionary model, the observations selecting against inappropriate theories by falsifying them. (Shea 2017) Thus, the term falsifiability is synonymous with testability. 

"My proposal is based upon an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability; an asymmetry which results from the logical form of universal statements. For these are never derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by singular statements. Consequently, it is possible by means of purely deductive inferences (with the help of the modus tollens of classical logic) to argue from the truth of singular statements to the falsity of universal statements. Such an argument to the falsity of universal statements is the only strictly deductive kind of inference that proceeds, as it were, in the 'inductive direction'; that is, from singular to universal statements." Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (K. R. Popper 2002) Popper pointed out that non-falsifiable claims are important in science. Contrary to intuition, non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into -and deductively generated byfalsifiable theories. Popper invented the notion of metaphysical research programs to name such non-falsifiable ideas. Unlike positivism, which considered statements to be meaningless if they cannot be verified or falsified, Popper argued that falsifiability is only a special case of the more general notion of criticality, even though he admitted that empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods by which theories can be criticized. Criticality, unlike falsifiability and therefore rationality, can be comprehensive (without logical boundaries), although this statement is controversial, even among the supporters of Popper's philosophy and rationalism.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: Karl Popper identified ‘falsifiability’ as the criterion in demarcating science from non-science. The method of induction, which uses the (debated) principle of uniformity of nature, was rejected by Popper. He instead suggested that a scientific theory cannot be ‘verifiable’ but only ‘falsifiable’; one counter-example to the claims made by the theory would falsify it. The paper conducts a survey of the extant literature to understand the concept, the methodology as suggested by Popper to operationalize the concept, and possible limitations, both conceptual and methodological. The extant literature points out inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. One recurring theme is that Popper, the deductivist, uses the much critiqued inductivistic method among his methodological suite.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: A major critique of Popper is that Popper's methodology of falsification is based on the despised (by Popper) inductive method (Derksen, 1985;Keita, 1989;Maxwell, 1972). This makes Popper's methodologies and assertions on falsifiability open to arguments. In any case, actual empirical science generally uses induction and actual scientific laws are situated in specific spatio-temporal contexts, thus countering Popper's critique that inductivists take a wild leap of faith when interpolating their findings to a universal context. The second critique, which Popper agreed with and replied by strengthening his framework, is the Duhem-Quine thesis: actual science considers a group of hypotheses and in tandem, and in such cases whereas individual hypothesis are falsifiable, the group is only confirmable and not falsifiable. Third, while Popper equated simplicity with falsifiabilty, researchers such as Goodman (1972) and Turney (1991) have picked up flaws in this argument as well. 

The paper takes a look at the various dimensions of the falsification criterion using a review of the extant literature. Various researchers have identified deficiencies in Popper's epistemology: also actual science works not necessarily in accordance with how Popper visualizes it. Nonetheless, Popper's falsifiability remains a very strong criterion, especially where research can be founded on value-laden assumptions such as in the social sciences including management, and scientists willing to subject their research to (Goodman, 1972) In the limited context, Goodman's argument holds. However, whether the second statement which is linguistically most simple is actually most simple or not may be open to argument. (Keita, 1989) Induction is a recurring theme in almost all critique of Popper's methodology. It is also a fact that induction does play a part in science, but that is not a problem with Popper's argument. With regard to Henry's law, the inductive approach cannot test for all possible situations in the restricted "temporal and spatial scope". Hence Popper's criterion of falsifiability as a criterion of demarcating science from non-science remains valid.

Title: Popper, kuhn, lakatos and aim-oriented empiricism
Snippet: As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.

snippet.text:
As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.

snippet.text:
Popper is a realist who argues that scientific theories follow the truth; he does not believe that empirical evidence can ever give us reason to believe that a theory is true or can be true. In this sense, Popper is a fallibilist, stating that it is impossible to justify the belief that a certain scientific theory is true. Where others see the progress of science by confirming the truth of private claims, Popper describes science as progressing on an evolutionary model, the observations selecting against inappropriate theories by falsifying them. (Shea 2017) Thus, the term falsifiability is synonymous with testability. 

"My proposal is based upon an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability; an asymmetry which results from the logical form of universal statements. For these are never derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by singular statements. Consequently, it is possible by means of purely deductive inferences (with the help of the modus tollens of classical logic) to argue from the truth of singular statements to the falsity of universal statements. Such an argument to the falsity of universal statements is the only strictly deductive kind of inference that proceeds, as it were, in the 'inductive direction'; that is, from singular to universal statements." Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (K. R. Popper 2002) Popper pointed out that non-falsifiable claims are important in science. Contrary to intuition, non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into -and deductively generated byfalsifiable theories. Popper invented the notion of metaphysical research programs to name such non-falsifiable ideas. Unlike positivism, which considered statements to be meaningless if they cannot be verified or falsified, Popper argued that falsifiability is only a special case of the more general notion of criticality, even though he admitted that empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods by which theories can be criticized. Criticality, unlike falsifiability and therefore rationality, can be comprehensive (without logical boundaries), although this statement is controversial, even among the supporters of Popper's philosophy and rationalism.

Thus, we will need to: 1) present arguments that K. Popper is an analytical philosopher, 2) consider his ideas of the objectivity of truth and criticism of relativism. Firstly, Karl Popper is in no way different from his friends the logical empiricists (logical positivists) in understanding and using the achievements of modern logic. Modern symbolic logic for K. documents.snippet: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

Title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
Snippet: It is worth pointing out that the Popperian critical discussion is not synonymous with agnosticism, a philosophical current that excludes all knowledge. To be clear, Popper did not claim that a truth and a theory cannot and should not be tested, accepted, and maintained as such. Rather he advocated for an open science that always assesses our vulnerabilities and attempts newer solutions. Popper did not propound a falsificationistic agnosticism, nor did he propound falsificationism that rejects all truths for the sake of falsifying. Using trial and error theory, he proposed falsifiability for the sake of open society. 

Tested theories and/or statements can govern our values and priorities under given circumstances and at a given point in time. "There must be some [emphasis in original] kind of minimum philosophy common to, at least, a great majority of those living in an Open Societya minimum common denominator, leaving room for the mutual toleration of otherwise most diverse philosophies and views" (Popper, 2008, p. 137). Open society does not mean a society void of minimum goals, values, and priorities with which to go about our daily lives. The question remains as to how far toleration should go. This remark takes us to the realization that falsifiability is only a portion of Popper's broader social program. 

With trial and error method, theories and human products are not holders of truth, but pointers of light in our endless search for greater light. The vulnerability of our theories is inter-subjectively assessed through the platform of critical discussion. Popper came to the thesis of falsifiability on the basis of the following grounds: 

The theory is criticised from very many standpoints in order to bring out those points which may be vulnerable. And the testing of the theory proceeds by its vulnerable sides to as severe an examination as possible. This again is the trial and error method. Theories are put forward tentatively and tried out… Its success depends mainly on three conditions, namely, that sufficiently many and sufficiently different theories are offered, and that sufficiently severe tests are made. In this way, we may secure, if we are lucky, the survival of the fittest theory by a process of elimination [emphasis mine].

Title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
Snippet: According to Popper, the distinct feature of scientific knowledge does not reside in the objective laws of nature and society, nor in the ability to verify and replicate the findings and suggested theories, but in the criticism of proposed theories and related concepts. Falsifiability comes through critical discussion, a method in which particular situations are examined on the basis of trial and error. As Keuth (2005) noted, "every universal statement is falsifiable [emphasis in original]" (p. 31) since there are no monolithic, universal truths. Scientific statements are and should be falsifiable under specific conditions and circumstances. When a statement's, proposition's, or an idea's falsifiability is acknowledged, this does not necessarily mean that these statements are useless. Nevertheless, scientists and policy-makers should be aware that the falsifiability of their claims (or some portion of their claims) is probable, instead of simply enjoying the ethos gained by the unchallenged use and occasional imposition of their claims. To be aware of the certainty of falsifiability requires an expectance that critical discussion will aim to falsify, or more precisely, to bring into greater focus the prone-to-error dimensions of obtained statements, decisions, or policies. Falsifiability, not predictability as is often suggested, represents the status of proposed theories, which in turn call for critical discussion in order to yield the most likely answer to problems posed. 

Without critical discussion, the Popperian falsifiability or falsification loses its purpose. While falsifiability has been widely known as the marker of Popper's work, it has obscured Popper's epistemological teachings, the most dominant theme of which is the trial and error method of knowledge. It is questionable that most discussions about the social sciences do not address the concept of falsifiability, and simply leave it to philosophers of science. As a result, the broader setting upon which falsifiability is anchored often escapes authors' attention. In sum, important ideas used by Popper (1959Popper ( , 1972) ) to explain falsifiability are trial and error theory of knowledge, natural selection, and survival of the fittest theory.

documents.snippet:
As everyone knows, Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by means of observation and experiment. Scientific theories cannot be verified by experience, but they can be falsified. Once a theory is falsified, scientists have the task of developing a potentially better theory, even more falsifiable than its predecessor, at least as ostensibly empirically successful as its predecessor, and such that it is corroborated where its predecessor was falsified. In order to be accepted (tentatively) as a part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must (at least) be empirically falsifiable. Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful, and may influence the direction of scientific research. There can even be what Popper has called "metaphysical research programmes" -programmes of research "indispensable for science, although their character is that of metaphysical or speculative physics rather than of scientific physics ... more in the nature of myths, or of dreams, than of science" (Popper, 1982, p. 165). For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as (conjectural) scientific knowledge, but they can influence ideas, choice of research aims and problems, in the context of scientific discovery. For further details see Popper (1959Popper ( , 1963Popper ( , 1983)). 

Popper defended two distinct versions of falsificationism which, echoing terminology of Maxwell (1998), I shall call bare and dressed falsificationism. According to bare falsificationism, defended in Popper (1959), only empirical considerations, and such things as the falsifiability of theories and degrees of falsifiability, decide what is to be accepted and rejected in science.

Testing hypotheses is one of the tenets behind scientific discovery.
