documents.title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
documents.snippet:
It is worth pointing out that the Popperian critical discussion is not synonymous with agnosticism, a philosophical current that excludes all knowledge. To be clear, Popper did not claim that a truth and a theory cannot and should not be tested, accepted, and maintained as such. Rather he advocated for an open science that always assesses our vulnerabilities and attempts newer solutions. Popper did not propound a falsificationistic agnosticism, nor did he propound falsificationism that rejects all truths for the sake of falsifying. Using trial and error theory, he proposed falsifiability for the sake of open society. 

Tested theories and/or statements can govern our values and priorities under given circumstances and at a given point in time. "There must be some [emphasis in original] kind of minimum philosophy common to, at least, a great majority of those living in an Open Societya minimum common denominator, leaving room for the mutual toleration of otherwise most diverse philosophies and views" (Popper, 2008, p. 137). Open society does not mean a society void of minimum goals, values, and priorities with which to go about our daily lives. The question remains as to how far toleration should go. This remark takes us to the realization that falsifiability is only a portion of Popper's broader social program. 

With trial and error method, theories and human products are not holders of truth, but pointers of light in our endless search for greater light. The vulnerability of our theories is inter-subjectively assessed through the platform of critical discussion. Popper came to the thesis of falsifiability on the basis of the following grounds: 

The theory is criticised from very many standpoints in order to bring out those points which may be vulnerable. And the testing of the theory proceeds by its vulnerable sides to as severe an examination as possible. This again is the trial and error method. Theories are put forward tentatively and tried out… Its success depends mainly on three conditions, namely, that sufficiently many and sufficiently different theories are offered, and that sufficiently severe tests are made. In this way, we may secure, if we are lucky, the survival of the fittest theory by a process of elimination [emphasis mine].

documents.title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
documents.snippet:
According to Popper, the distinct feature of scientific knowledge does not reside in the objective laws of nature and society, nor in the ability to verify and replicate the findings and suggested theories, but in the criticism of proposed theories and related concepts. Falsifiability comes through critical discussion, a method in which particular situations are examined on the basis of trial and error. As Keuth (2005) noted, "every universal statement is falsifiable [emphasis in original]" (p. 31) since there are no monolithic, universal truths. Scientific statements are and should be falsifiable under specific conditions and circumstances. When a statement's, proposition's, or an idea's falsifiability is acknowledged, this does not necessarily mean that these statements are useless. Nevertheless, scientists and policy-makers should be aware that the falsifiability of their claims (or some portion of their claims) is probable, instead of simply enjoying the ethos gained by the unchallenged use and occasional imposition of their claims. To be aware of the certainty of falsifiability requires an expectance that critical discussion will aim to falsify, or more precisely, to bring into greater focus the prone-to-error dimensions of obtained statements, decisions, or policies. Falsifiability, not predictability as is often suggested, represents the status of proposed theories, which in turn call for critical discussion in order to yield the most likely answer to problems posed. 

Without critical discussion, the Popperian falsifiability or falsification loses its purpose. While falsifiability has been widely known as the marker of Popper's work, it has obscured Popper's epistemological teachings, the most dominant theme of which is the trial and error method of knowledge. It is questionable that most discussions about the social sciences do not address the concept of falsifiability, and simply leave it to philosophers of science. As a result, the broader setting upon which falsifiability is anchored often escapes authors' attention. In sum, important ideas used by Popper (1959Popper ( , 1972) ) to explain falsifiability are trial and error theory of knowledge, natural selection, and survival of the fittest theory.

Below is a synthesis of why feminism and psychoanalysis face analogous difficulties with Popperian testability, despite addressing different subject matters.

1) Popperian demarcation and its conceptual limits
Popper proposed falsifiability as the asymmetrical criterion for demarcating scientific from non‑scientific claims: universal theories can be contradicted by singular observations through deductive inference (modus tollens), while verification of universals is impossible; thus falsifiability is synonymous with testability and the engine of scientific progress via “critical severity.” <cite id="7995c8a7-0">Popper’s falsifiability is an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability, with universal statements derivable from singular statements yet contradictible by them, making deductive inference via modus tollens the core of testing; non‑falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into falsifiable theories as “metaphysical research programs,” and falsifiability is a species of criticality rather than the sole mark of meaning</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-1">Falsifiability treats a single counterexample as logically decisive; induction is untenable, and theories are preferred on the basis of being most easily falsifiable; falsifiability alone demarcates science from non‑science</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-2">Science proceeds by empirically falsifiable conjectures subjected to severe attempts at falsification; non‑falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide research but not be part of scientific knowledge, and Popper distinguished “bare” falsificationism from “dressed” falsificationism in which metaphysical underpinnings can shape science</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-3">Popper’s trial‑and‑error, natural‑selection model makes “objectivity” a matter of critical method, with inter‑subjective critique of taken‑for‑granted philosophical underpinnings that can bias research</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-4">Verificationism’s requirement that universal laws be completely verifiable is too strict, so Popper substituted falsifiability (negative tests), though this downplays affirmative existential hypotheses; Popper critiqued inductive logic and held that corroboration grows from survival of severe tests</cite>.

Crucially, falsifiability hinges on: (a) singular, negative empirical tests that disconfirm universal claims; (b) predictive, theory‑external criteria for adjudication; and (c) a naturalistic model of explanation. These constraints strain frameworks that are interpretive, non‑predictive, or socially reflexive.

2) Feminism: post‑positivist epistemology, standpoint, and the testability question
Feminist epistemologies commonly reject foundationalist/positivist demarcation and emphasize that knowledge is socially embedded, power‑laden, and historically situated. This entails: evidence and interpretation are theory‑laden; concepts such as gender, patriarchy, and oppression are not merely descriptive but normatively and politically inflected; and standpoint shapes both questions and methods. <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist standpoint epistemology challenges traditional conceptions of rationality and objectivity, facing charges of reduction to politics/power and drift toward relativism, yet articulates serious post‑positivist challenges to mainstream epistemology</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-0">Critical reviews of falsifiability highlight ambiguities and methodological tensions; Popper’s metric of “most falsifiable = most scientific” collapses into a hierarchy of desiderata that invites critique</cite>.

Within this frame, testability faces two linked problems. First, social embeddedness and ethical/justice stakes make the selection, interpretation, and weighting of evidence indeterminate. Empirical data are filtered by standpoint and by commitments to social change, so “falsification” of gendered theories often runs up against re‑interpretation, contextual defense, and value‑laden adjudication rather than singular disconfirming facts. Second, feminist ontologies treat structures like patriarchy as systemic, discursive, and practice‑constituting, not merely causal regularities waiting to be statistically rejected; this makes “counterexamples” ambiguous and underdetermined. Standpoint accounts even suggest comparative epistemic advantage: oppressed groups are more reliable than non‑oppressed ones about domains of oppression, which entrenches reflexivity and contextuality in evidence evaluation rather than Popperian neutrality. <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint reliability claims posit that women are more reliable truth‑trackers about gender relations and that social standing shapes reasons and recognition of reasons, yielding comparative epistemic privilege and reliability relative to a domain</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-1">An “epistemology of the South” advances intersectional, anti‑colonial feminist frameworks to overcome epistemological barriers, underscoring that prior epistemic tools may fail to end gender violence, thus motivating frameworks attuned to power and colonial practice</cite>.

3) Psychoanalysis: hermeneutic explanation, non‑predictive laws, and Popper’s critique
Psychoanalysis has been criticized for combining “irrational” unconscious contents with causal metapsychological laws, yielding a dual epistemology that mixes hermeneutic reconstruction and purported natural‑science explanatory aims. Hermeneutic reconstructions are retroactive, co‑constructed, and non‑predictive; hence they are hard to falsify deductively, a central point of Popperian demarcation. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic understanding often proceeds by hermeneutic, circular processes where initial understandings are improved via co‑construction of meaning through transference; purely hermeneutic explanations act retroactively and do not make predictions, making them inherently difficult to falsify, an issue emphasized by Popper</cite>.

Lacan explicitly contests Popper’s claim that the unconscious is “insensible to contradiction,” arguing that psychoanalysis is not inductive and does not require verificationism. He invokes Gödel’s incompleteness and non‑Euclidean geometry to show that formal systems necessarily entail undecidable/contradictory propositions, and he claims the unconscious, structured like language, is structurally incoherent in ways that are not eliminable by empirical refutation. Lacan also attempts to show that Freud’s metapsychology can be articulated in formal, axiomatic terms, resisting Popperian falsification. <cite id="3ad40d8c-0">Lacan replies to Popper’s critique that psychoanalysis “transcendentalises” the unconscious by asserting Freud’s thesis that it is “insensible to contradiction,” arguing that psychoanalysis cannot be reduced to induction and that falsificationism cannot capture its logic</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-4">Lacan leverages Gödel and non‑Euclidean advances to show that contradiction is fatality for formal systems; the unconscious, structured as language, is complete in specific formal senses and thus exhibits primary‑process properties incompatible with empirical decidability</cite>.

Popper’s critique is often summarized as an accusation that psychoanalysis allows only confirming evidence and is “at best pseudo‑scientific.” Yet Popper also distinguishes “irreducible” metapsychological concepts (e.g., “drive,” “instinct”) that are not verifiable yet can be embedded within a research program whose falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses enable empirical progress; Grünbaum and others argue that Popper’s demarcation fails sociologically and that psychoanalysis has indeed been falsified in specific instances and contains falsifiable claims. <cite id="3ad40d8c-3">Popper labeled psychoanalysis “at best a pseudo‑science and at worst complete nonsense,” criticizing its verificationist, confirming‑evidence approach and arguing it fails demarcation; Grünbaum counters that psychoanalysis can be falsified (e.g., Freud’s 1915 paranoia paper) and that Popper’s demarcation is sociologically limited</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Popper grouped psychoanalysis with Marxism and Adler as pseudosciences due to their “explanatory everything, confirm everything” bias, yet later critics (Laudan, Mahner, Pigliucci) argue psychoanalysis does include falsifiable claims and that falsificationism itself cannot solve demarcation; Lakatos questions whether falsifiability distinguishes science</cite>.

4) Comparative mechanisms: why similar demarcation problems arise
Despite different objects (social structures vs. unconscious structures), feminism and psychoanalysis share methodological features that strain Popperian testability:

- Interpretive, non‑predictive ontology: both treat their targets as systems of meaning and practice rather than merely causal regularities; concepts (patriarchy; unconscious/“Real,” drive) are not exhausted by observable singularities, making disconfirmation hinge on contested interpretations of language, discourse, and symptom. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic hermeneutic explanations are retroactive and non‑predictive, hence inherently difficult to falsify</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint epistemology locates epistemic privilege and reliability within social position, making evidence interpretation comparatively situated rather than Popperianly neutral</cite>.

- Reflexivity of the knower and ethical/political stakes: researchers themselves are situated within, or in close relation to, the domain (clinicians to patients; feminists to oppressed groups), which shapes question selection, measurement, and interpretation. This undermines Popper’s demand for theory‑external, value‑neutral falsification and instead produces a dynamic of critique, reinterpretation, and normative adjudication. <cite id="7995c8a7-3">Popper emphasizes inter‑subjective critical discussion and the need to criticize taken‑for‑granted philosophical underpinnings precisely because they can unconsciously bias research</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist epistemologies confront “reduction to politics/power” and relativism worries, yet insist on post‑positivist challenges to truth and objectivity, situating knowledge in power relations</cite>.

- Holism and metaphysical programs: both fields embed unfalsifiable, guiding frameworks (e.g., patriarchy as a social ontology; Freud’s structural model of the mind) alongside falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses. Popper allows such metaphysical programs to orient research while insisting that only falsifiable claims count as scientific; however, in practice, the holistic interweaving of theory and interpretation makes disconfirming tests rare, ambiguous, or re‑interpretive rather than decisive. <cite id="7995c8a7-2">Non‑falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide research (metaphysical research programs) without entering as part of scientific knowledge proper</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Critics argue psychoanalysis contains falsifiable claims and that falsificationist demarcation fails, complicating Popper’s separation of “science” and “pseudoscience”</cite>.

- Hermeneutic vs. naturalistic demarcation: Popper’s ideal requires negative empirical tests that decisively refute universal claims, privileging predictive, law‑like models. Feminist and psychoanalytic methods often prioritize interpretive, case‑based, and discursive analysis, where “falsification” amounts to re‑reading or paradigm shift rather than a singular disconfirming event; this mismatch explains recurring demarcation anxieties. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Hermeneutic psychoanalysis co‑constructs meaning and lacks predictive falsibility, a core Popperian demand</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-0">Ambiguities in falsifiability’s operationalization and the hierarchy “most falsifiable = most scientific” show Popper’s criterion is methodologically contested</cite>.

5) Nuance: empirical turns, auxiliary falsifiable markers, and research programs
Both fields have responded by tightening auxiliary empirical tests. Psychoanalysis has sought causal, testable metapsychological laws and quantitative/clinical criteria; philosophers note that purely hermeneutic retroactivity is not the only option, and specific falsifications have occurred, though disagreement persists. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Freud aimed to combine qualitative hermeneutics with quantitative causal theory; purely hermeneutic explanations are epistemologically problematic because they lack predictive falsifiability, yet psychoanalysis historically aspired to both</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Grünbaum shows concrete ways Freud’s theories could be falsified and concedes Popper’s critique spurred accountability; nevertheless, psychoanalysis has indeed been falsified and contains falsifiable components</cite>. Feminism has drawn on science and technology studies, feminist empiricism, and standpoint‑informed methods to articulate research programs that remain critical and interpretive but specify testable consequences (e.g., in medicine, biology, and education), while defending that standpoint knowledge is not less, but differently, “objective.” <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist epistemologies articulate serious challenges to mainstream conceptions of rationality and objectivity, yet emphasize that their methods are not the only ones pushing post‑positivist epistemology</cite>.

Conclusion
Feminism and psychoanalysis mirror each other’s demarcation challenges because both embed interpretive, socially and ethically situated ontologies and methods that resist Popperian predictive falsification. Their concepts (patriarchy; unconscious, drive, Real) are systemic and linguistic rather than merely causal regularities, their knowledge production is reflexive and co‑constitutive, and their programs interweave metaphysical frameworks with auxiliary empirical tests that are many‑sided and context‑bound. Popper’s ideal of decisive negative tests fits best to narrow natural‑science laws; the fields’ hermeneutic and critical orientations push demarcation toward sociological, historical, and philosophical adjudication rather than singular refutation. <cite id="7995c8a7-0">Popper’s asymmetry of falsifiability versus verifiability and allowance of metaphysical programs set the stage for such tensions</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic hermeneutic retroactivity and lack of prediction make falsification difficult</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint epistemology locates epistemic privilege and reliability in social position, not Popperian neutrality</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Critics show psychoanalysis has falsifiable components and that falsificationism’s demarcation is sociologically limited</cite>.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

Title: Causation in Psychoanalysis
Snippet: During psychoanalytic therapy, analyst, and client aim to understand the analyst's mental and affective life. Many aspects of this inner life appear initially absurd and paradoxical; the belief that even (and particularly) apparent nonsensical aspects are relevant and may in principle be understood is a cornerstone of psychoanalytic theory (Brenner, 1955). The process of understanding these phenomena has been conceptualized as "hermeneutic" -as a circular process by which an initial and superficial understanding is incrementally improved as analyst and client co-construct meaning through conscious and unconscious affective transference. Scientific researchers also search to understand seemingly random phenomena when they attempt to find regularities in their data. These regularities may then be used to generate predictions for future experiments and to build hypotheses about underlying causal laws. Freud throughout his life maintained the ideal to combine these two levels of investigation -to find scientific explanations for the conscious and unconscious psychic contents and somatic symptoms that he observed in his patients. In this combination of qualitative hermeneutics with quantitative theories, Freudian psychoanalysis had a unique dual epistemological character (Ricoeur, 1970). Many philosophers (e.g., Habermas, 2005) and psychoanalysts (e.g., Spence, 1982;Thomä and Kächele, 2006) criticized the biological ancestry of Freudian psychoanalysis and its attempt to find "metapsychological" laws of psychic life that resemble the explanations in the natural sciences; instead, they suggested to ground psychoanalysis on a purely hermeneutic basis. 

However, purely hermeneutic explanations are epistemologically problematic because they typically act in a retroactive manner -they attempt to explain consisting affects, psychic contents, and somatic symptoms, but do not make predictions about future developments. Therefore, purely hermeneutic hypotheses are inherently difficult to falsify, which has been extensively criticized by philosophers such as Popper (1963). This problem would not occur if hermeneutic reconstructions were (at least in principle) consistent with causal explanations -in this case, one could predict that removal of the cause should alter its effect as well.
</snippet>

I found that those of my friends who were admirers of Marx, Freud, and Adler, were impressed by a number of points common to these theories, and especially by their apparent explanatory power. Below is a synthesis of why feminism and psychoanalysis face analogous difficulties with Popperian testability, despite addressing different subject matters.

1) Popperian demarcation and its conceptual limits
Popper proposed falsifiability as the asymmetrical criterion for demarcating scientific from non‑scientific claims: universal theories can be contradicted by singular observations through deductive inference (modus tollens), while verification of universals is impossible; thus falsifiability is synonymous with testability and the engine of scientific progress via “critical severity.” <cite id="7995c8a7-0">Popper’s falsifiability is an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability, with universal statements derivable from singular statements yet contradictible by them, making deductive inference via modus tollens the core of testing; non‑falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into falsifiable theories as “metaphysical research programs,” and falsifiability is a species of criticality rather than the sole mark of meaning</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-1">Falsifiability treats a single counterexample as logically decisive; induction is untenable, and theories are preferred on the basis of being most easily falsifiable; falsifiability alone demarcates science from non‑science</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-2">Science proceeds by empirically falsifiable conjectures subjected to severe attempts at falsification; non‑falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide research but not be part of scientific knowledge, and Popper distinguished “bare” falsificationism from “dressed” falsificationism in which metaphysical underpinnings can shape science</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-3">Popper’s trial‑and‑error, natural‑selection model makes “objectivity” a matter of critical method, with inter‑subjective critique of taken‑for‑granted philosophical underpinnings that can bias research</cite> <cite id="7995c8a7-4">Verificationism’s requirement that universal laws be completely verifiable is too strict, so Popper substituted falsifiability (negative tests), though this downplays affirmative existential hypotheses; Popper critiqued inductive logic and held that corroboration grows from survival of severe tests</cite>.

Crucially, falsifiability hinges on: (a) singular, negative empirical tests that disconfirm universal claims; (b) predictive, theory‑external criteria for adjudication; and (c) a naturalistic model of explanation. These constraints strain frameworks that are interpretive, non‑predictive, or socially reflexive.

2) Feminism: post‑positivist epistemology, standpoint, and the testability question
Feminist epistemologies commonly reject foundationalist/positivist demarcation and emphasize that knowledge is socially embedded, power‑laden, and historically situated. This entails: evidence and interpretation are theory‑laden; concepts such as gender, patriarchy, and oppression are not merely descriptive but normatively and politically inflected; and standpoint shapes both questions and methods. <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist standpoint epistemology challenges traditional conceptions of rationality and objectivity, facing charges of reduction to politics/power and drift toward relativism, yet articulates serious post‑positivist challenges to mainstream epistemology</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-0">Critical reviews of falsifiability highlight ambiguities and methodological tensions; Popper’s metric of “most falsifiable = most scientific” collapses into a hierarchy of desiderata that invites critique</cite>.

Within this frame, testability faces two linked problems. First, social embeddedness and ethical/justice stakes make the selection, interpretation, and weighting of evidence indeterminate. Empirical data are filtered by standpoint and by commitments to social change, so “falsification” of gendered theories often runs up against re‑interpretation, contextual defense, and value‑laden adjudication rather than singular disconfirming facts. Second, feminist ontologies treat structures like patriarchy as systemic, discursive, and practice‑constituting, not merely causal regularities waiting to be statistically rejected; this makes “counterexamples” ambiguous and underdetermined. Standpoint accounts even suggest comparative epistemic advantage: oppressed groups are more reliable than non‑oppressed ones about domains of oppression, which entrenches reflexivity and contextuality in evidence evaluation rather than Popperian neutrality. <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint reliability claims posit that women are more reliable truth‑trackers about gender relations and that social standing shapes reasons and recognition of reasons, yielding comparative epistemic privilege and reliability relative to a domain</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-1">An “epistemology of the South” advances intersectional, anti‑colonial feminist frameworks to overcome epistemological barriers, underscoring that prior epistemic tools may fail to end gender violence, thus motivating frameworks attuned to power and colonial practice</cite>.

3) Psychoanalysis: hermeneutic explanation, non‑predictive laws, and Popper’s critique
Psychoanalysis has been criticized for combining “irrational” unconscious contents with causal metapsychological laws, yielding a dual epistemology that mixes hermeneutic reconstruction and purported natural‑science explanatory aims. Hermeneutic reconstructions are retroactive, co‑constructed, and non‑predictive; hence they are hard to falsify deductively, a central point of Popperian demarcation. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic understanding often proceeds by hermeneutic, circular processes where initial understandings are improved via co‑construction of meaning through transference; purely hermeneutic explanations act retroactively and do not make predictions, making them inherently difficult to falsify, an issue emphasized by Popper</cite>.

Lacan explicitly contests Popper’s claim that the unconscious is “insensible to contradiction,” arguing that psychoanalysis is not inductive and does not require verificationism. He invokes Gödel’s incompleteness and non‑Euclidean geometry to show that formal systems necessarily entail undecidable/contradictory propositions, and he claims the unconscious, structured like language, is structurally incoherent in ways that are not eliminable by empirical refutation. Lacan also attempts to show that Freud’s metapsychology can be articulated in formal, axiomatic terms, resisting Popperian falsification. <cite id="3ad40d8c-0">Lacan replies to Popper’s critique that psychoanalysis “transcendentalises” the unconscious by asserting Freud’s thesis that it is “insensible to contradiction,” arguing that psychoanalysis cannot be reduced to induction and that falsificationism cannot capture its logic</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-4">Lacan leverages Gödel and non‑Euclidean advances to show that contradiction is fatality for formal systems; the unconscious, structured as language, is complete in specific formal senses and thus exhibits primary‑process properties incompatible with empirical decidability</cite>.

Popper’s critique is often summarized as an accusation that psychoanalysis allows only confirming evidence and is “at best pseudo‑scientific.” Yet Popper also distinguishes “irreducible” metapsychological concepts (e.g., “drive,” “instinct”) that are not verifiable yet can be embedded within a research program whose falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses enable empirical progress; Grünbaum and others argue that Popper’s demarcation fails sociologically and that psychoanalysis has indeed been falsified in specific instances and contains falsifiable claims. <cite id="3ad40d8c-3">Popper labeled psychoanalysis “at best a pseudo‑science and at worst complete nonsense,” criticizing its verificationist, confirming‑evidence approach and arguing it fails demarcation; Grünbaum counters that psychoanalysis can be falsified (e.g., Freud’s 1915 paranoia paper) and that Popper’s demarcation is sociologically limited</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Popper grouped psychoanalysis with Marxism and Adler as pseudosciences due to their “explanatory everything, confirm everything” bias, yet later critics (Laudan, Mahner, Pigliucci) argue psychoanalysis does include falsifiable claims and that falsificationism itself cannot solve demarcation; Lakatos questions whether falsifiability distinguishes science</cite>.

4) Comparative mechanisms: why similar demarcation problems arise
Despite different objects (social structures vs. unconscious structures), feminism and psychoanalysis share methodological features that strain Popperian testability:

- Interpretive, non‑predictive ontology: both treat their targets as systems of meaning and practice rather than merely causal regularities; concepts (patriarchy; unconscious/“Real,” drive) are not exhausted by observable singularities, making disconfirmation hinge on contested interpretations of language, discourse, and symptom. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic hermeneutic explanations are retroactive and non‑predictive, hence inherently difficult to falsify</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint epistemology locates epistemic privilege and reliability within social position, making evidence interpretation comparatively situated rather than Popperianly neutral</cite>.

- Reflexivity of the knower and ethical/political stakes: researchers themselves are situated within, or in close relation to, the domain (clinicians to patients; feminists to oppressed groups), which shapes question selection, measurement, and interpretation. This undermines Popper’s demand for theory‑external, value‑neutral falsification and instead produces a dynamic of critique, reinterpretation, and normative adjudication. <cite id="7995c8a7-3">Popper emphasizes inter‑subjective critical discussion and the need to criticize taken‑for‑granted philosophical underpinnings precisely because they can unconsciously bias research</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist epistemologies confront “reduction to politics/power” and relativism worries, yet insist on post‑positivist challenges to truth and objectivity, situating knowledge in power relations</cite>.

- Holism and metaphysical programs: both fields embed unfalsifiable, guiding frameworks (e.g., patriarchy as a social ontology; Freud’s structural model of the mind) alongside falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses. Popper allows such metaphysical programs to orient research while insisting that only falsifiable claims count as scientific; however, in practice, the holistic interweaving of theory and interpretation makes disconfirming tests rare, ambiguous, or re‑interpretive rather than decisive. <cite id="7995c8a7-2">Non‑falsifiable metaphysical theses can guide research (metaphysical research programs) without entering as part of scientific knowledge proper</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Critics argue psychoanalysis contains falsifiable claims and that falsificationist demarcation fails, complicating Popper’s separation of “science” and “pseudoscience”</cite>.

- Hermeneutic vs. naturalistic demarcation: Popper’s ideal requires negative empirical tests that decisively refute universal claims, privileging predictive, law‑like models. Feminist and psychoanalytic methods often prioritize interpretive, case‑based, and discursive analysis, where “falsification” amounts to re‑reading or paradigm shift rather than a singular disconfirming event; this mismatch explains recurring demarcation anxieties. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Hermeneutic psychoanalysis co‑constructs meaning and lacks predictive falsibility, a core Popperian demand</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-0">Ambiguities in falsifiability’s operationalization and the hierarchy “most falsifiable = most scientific” show Popper’s criterion is methodologically contested</cite>.

5) Nuance: empirical turns, auxiliary falsifiable markers, and research programs
Both fields have responded by tightening auxiliary empirical tests. Psychoanalysis has sought causal, testable metapsychological laws and quantitative/clinical criteria; philosophers note that purely hermeneutic retroactivity is not the only option, and specific falsifications have occurred, though disagreement persists. <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Freud aimed to combine qualitative hermeneutics with quantitative causal theory; purely hermeneutic explanations are epistemologically problematic because they lack predictive falsifiability, yet psychoanalysis historically aspired to both</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Grünbaum shows concrete ways Freud’s theories could be falsified and concedes Popper’s critique spurred accountability; nevertheless, psychoanalysis has indeed been falsified and contains falsifiable components</cite>. Feminism has drawn on science and technology studies, feminist empiricism, and standpoint‑informed methods to articulate research programs that remain critical and interpretive but specify testable consequences (e.g., in medicine, biology, and education), while defending that standpoint knowledge is not less, but differently, “objective.” <cite id="d98b3d35-4">Feminist epistemologies articulate serious challenges to mainstream conceptions of rationality and objectivity, yet emphasize that their methods are not the only ones pushing post‑positivist epistemology</cite>.

Conclusion
Feminism and psychoanalysis mirror each other’s demarcation challenges because both embed interpretive, socially and ethically situated ontologies and methods that resist Popperian predictive falsification. Their concepts (patriarchy; unconscious, drive, Real) are systemic and linguistic rather than merely causal regularities, their knowledge production is reflexive and co‑constitutive, and their programs interweave metaphysical frameworks with auxiliary empirical tests that are many‑sided and context‑bound. Popper’s ideal of decisive negative tests fits best to narrow natural‑science laws; the fields’ hermeneutic and critical orientations push demarcation toward sociological, historical, and philosophical adjudication rather than singular refutation. <cite id="7995c8a7-0">Popper’s asymmetry of falsifiability versus verifiability and allowance of metaphysical programs set the stage for such tensions</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-1">Psychoanalytic hermeneutic retroactivity and lack of prediction make falsification difficult</cite> <cite id="d98b3d35-3">Standpoint epistemology locates epistemic privilege and reliability in social position, not Popperian neutrality</cite> <cite id="3ad40d8c-2">Critics show psychoanalysis has falsifiable components and that falsificationism’s demarcation is sociologically limited</cite>.</answer>

Title: Science and Pseudoscience - Falsifiability
Snippet: Popper is a realist who argues that scientific theories follow the truth; he does not believe that empirical evidence can ever give us reason to believe that a theory is true or can be true. In this sense, Popper is a fallibilist, stating that it is impossible to justify the belief that a certain scientific theory is true. Where others see the progress of science by confirming the truth of private claims, Popper describes science as progressing on an evolutionary model, the observations selecting against inappropriate theories by falsifying them. (Shea 2017) Thus, the term falsifiability is synonymous with testability. 

"My proposal is based upon an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability; an asymmetry which results from the logical form of universal statements. For these are never derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by singular statements. Consequently, it is possible by means of purely deductive inferences (with the help of the modus tollens of classical logic) to argue from the truth of singular statements to the falsity of universal statements. Such an argument to the falsity of universal statements is the only strictly deductive kind of inference that proceeds, as it were, in the 'inductive direction'; that is, from singular to universal statements." Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (K. R. Popper 2002) Popper pointed out that non-falsifiable claims are important in science. Contrary to intuition, non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into -and deductively generated byfalsifiable theories. Popper invented the notion of metaphysical research programs to name such non-falsifiable ideas. Unlike positivism, which considered statements to be meaningless if they cannot be verified or falsified, Popper argued that falsifiability is only a special case of the more general notion of criticality, even though he admitted that empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods by which theories can be criticized. Criticality, unlike falsifiability and therefore rationality, can be comprehensive (without logical boundaries), although this statement is controversial, even among the supporters of Popper's philosophy and rationalism.

Title: Dynamic Knowledge—A Century of Evolution
Snippet: The term "falsifiable" means that if a hypothesis is false this can be shown by observation or experiment. Logically, no number of positive outcomes at the level of experimental testing can confirm a scientific theory, but a single counter-example is logically decisive: it shows the theory, from which the implication is derived, to be false. The shortcomings of induction therefore led Popper to the development of a deductive method of testing. He held that one should rationally prefer the least likely (simplest, most easily falsifiable) theory that explains known facts. It is impossible, Popper argued, to ensure that a theory is true; it is more important that its falsity can be detected as easily as possible. We cannot know with certainty what is always true, only what is not. 

The demarcation between scientific and transcendental problems has been an important question in philosophy. In induction logic, the criterion for the demarcation of the empirical sciences from mathematics, logic, and metaphysics is definitive, because the logical form of its statements is such that their verification or falsification is finally decidable. This is not the case in the hypothetical-deductive theory of knowledge. Popper is a realist who argues that scientific theories follow the truth; he does not believe that empirical evidence can ever give us reason to believe that a theory is true or can be true. In this sense, Popper is a fallibilist, stating that it is impossible to justify the belief that a certain scientific theory is true. Where others see the progress of science by confirming the truth of private claims, Popper describes science as progressing on an evolutionary model, the observations selecting against inappropriate theories by falsifying them. (Shea 2017) Thus, the term falsifiability is synonymous with testability. 

"My proposal is based upon an asymmetry between verifiability and falsifiability; an asymmetry which results from the logical form of universal statements. For these are never derivable from singular statements but can be contradicted by singular statements. Consequently, it is possible by means of purely deductive inferences (with the help of the modus tollens of classical logic) to argue from the truth of singular statements to the falsity of universal statements. Such an argument to the falsity of universal statements is the only strictly deductive kind of inference that proceeds, as it were, in the 'inductive direction'; that is, from singular to universal statements." Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (K. R. Popper 2002) Popper pointed out that non-falsifiable claims are important in science. Contrary to intuition, non-falsifiable assertions can be incorporated into -and deductively generated byfalsifiable theories. Popper invented the notion of metaphysical research programs to name such non-falsifiable ideas. Unlike positivism, which considered statements to be meaningless if they cannot be verified or falsified, Popper argued that falsifiability is only a special case of the more general notion of criticality, even though he admitted that empirical rejection is one of the most effective methods by which theories can be criticized. Criticality, unlike falsifiability and therefore rationality, can be comprehensive (without logical boundaries), although this statement is controversial, even among the supporters of Popper's philosophy and rationalism.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

Title: Epistemologies of violence against women. A proposal from the South
Snippet: Are we using the appropriate conceptual framework in order to terminate the practice of control and violence against women? Maybe we are not applying the right epistemic framework to understand this type of violence. What epistemic change do we need to understand the nature of gender violence? The proposal of an epistemology of the South is presented as a useful logical alliance of an intersectional vision of feminisms that may allow us to understand and transform the reality of violence against women. Authors such as Boaventura de Sousa Santos and Rita Segato are the ones this article follow in order to present a feminism able to overcome the epistemological barriers and colonial practices that still exist today.

Title: An Analysis of the Falsification Criterion of Karl Popper: A Critical Review
Snippet: Karl Popper identified ‘falsifiability’ as the criterion in demarcating science from non-science. The method of induction, which uses the (debated) principle of uniformity of nature, was rejected by Popper. He instead suggested that a scientific theory cannot be ‘verifiable’ but only ‘falsifiable’; one counter-example to the claims made by the theory would falsify it. The paper conducts a survey of the extant literature to understand the concept, the methodology as suggested by Popper to operationalize the concept, and possible limitations, both conceptual and methodological. The extant literature points out inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. One recurring theme is that Popper, the deductivist, uses the much critiqued inductivistic method among his methodological suite.

Title: The Epistemic Role of Outlaw Emotions
Snippet: I do not have space to do so here. See Brun Doğuoğlu, and Kuenzle (2008), Pelser (2014) and Sreenivasan (2018) for arguments to this effect.

That reliabilism and standpoint epistemology are particularly compatible has been noted by Kitcher (1994), Michaelian (2008) and Srinivasan (2020). epistemology seems prima facie promising in dealing with outlaw emotion cases given that JV and MV failed to incorporate social components into their accounts. Here I sketch how such an account might be developed using insights from standpoint epistemology in particular. A consideration of standpoint epistemology lies beyond the scope of this paper. 25 For our purposes we will take the main insight from standpoint epistemology to be the claim that oppressed individuals are in a position of epistemic privilege regarding their own oppression. The claim is not that being a member of an oppressed group is necessary or sufficient to gaining knowledge about the relevant domain of oppression, but rather that oppressed groups are better positioned to gain knowledge about their oppression given their particular social standing. 26 This is because social positions make a difference to what reasons agents have, as well as their dispositions to recognize reasons as reasons (Toole 2019). 

What seems natural to suggest then, is that one's social standing makes one a more reliable truth tracker relative to a certain domain. So, women will more reliably track the reality of society's gender relations, while people of colour will more reliably track truths regarding racial relations. Reliability here is comparative, the oppressed are more reliable, as compared to those who are not oppressed, at tracking truths relative to a relevant domain. 27 Kitcher has made a similar point and says that 'reliabilists should insist that some standpoints are better or worse than others with respect to certain types of propositions ' (1994: 125). 28 This gives us the following reliability claim about social positions: 

Standpoint Reliability (SR): Oppressed individuals are more reliable at generating true beliefs regarding particular domain(s) of oppression. 

Outlaw emotions are one relevant type of experience that can generate beliefs.

Title: Knowledge for a Common World? On the Place of Feminist Epistemology in Philosophy of Education

snippet.text: Derksen (1985) critiques Popper's concept of falsifiability and calls it 'fake cement' to achieve methodological unity in the philosophy of science. He examines Popper's epistemology and suggests that apparently the concept of falsifiability leads to a 'great chain' of concepts, all linked to falsifiability. A wide variety of desiderata, such as most falsifiable, most testable, most informative and the best corroborated are all achievable simultaneously. However Derksen (1985) claims that there are inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. As a result, the great chain disintegrates along with the methodological unanimity that goes with it. Derksen (1985) examines the great chain in detail. According to Popper, any learning is possible through falsifying our guesses. Hence the first claim in this chain is: "only from our mistakes can we learn". This is actually falsifiability, or criticizabilty, a broader term. Now, if learning is possible only through mistakes, scientific theories should be open to empirical falsification. Generalizing this, a more falsifiable theory has a better probability of being falsified, and hence is more scientific. Or in other words, the scientific character of a theory is measurable and falsifiabilty is its metric.

snippet.text: Are we using the appropriate conceptual framework in order to terminate the practice of control and violence against women? Maybe we are not applying the right epistemic framework to understand this type of violence. What epistemic change do we need to understand the nature of gender violence? The proposal of an epistemology of the South is presented as a useful logical alliance of an intersectional vision of feminisms that may allow us to understand and transform the reality of violence against women. Authors such as Boaventura de Sousa Santos and Rita Segato are the ones this article follow in order to present a feminism able to overcome the epistemological barriers and colonial practices that still exist today.

snippet.text: Karl Popper identified ‘falsifiability’ as the criterion in demarcating science from non-science. The method of induction, which uses the (debated) principle of uniformity of nature, was rejected by Popper. He instead suggested that a scientific theory cannot be ‘verifiable’ but only ‘falsifiable’; one counter-example to the claims made by the theory would falsify it. The paper conducts a survey of the extant literature to understand the concept, the methodology as suggested by Popper to operationalize the concept, and possible limitations, both conceptual and methodological. The extant literature points out inherent ambiguities in the Popperian concept of falsifiabilty. One recurring theme is that Popper, the deductivist, uses the much critiqued inductivistic method among his methodological suite.

That reliabilism and standpoint epistemology are particularly compatible has been noted by Kitcher (1994), Michaelian (2008) and Srinivasan (2020). epistemology seems prima facie promising in dealing with outlaw emotion cases given that JV and MV failed to incorporate social components into their accounts. Here I sketch how such an account might be developed using insights from standpoint epistemology in particular. A consideration of standpoint epistemology lies beyond the scope of this paper. 25 For our purposes we will take the main insight from standpoint epistemology to be the claim that oppressed individuals are in a position of epistemic privilege regarding their own oppression. The claim is not that being a member of an oppressed group is necessary or sufficient to gaining knowledge about the relevant domain of oppression, but rather that oppressed groups are better positioned to gain knowledge about their oppression given their particular social standing. 26 This is because social positions make a difference to what reasons agents have, as well as their dispositions to recognize reasons as reasons (Toole 2019). 

What seems natural to suggest then, is that one's social standing makes one a more reliable truth tracker relative to a certain domain. So, women will more reliably track the reality of society's gender relations, while people of colour will more reliably track truths regarding racial relations. Reliability here is comparative, the oppressed are more reliable, as compared to those who are not oppressed, at tracking truths relative to a relevant domain. 27 Kitcher has made a similar point and says that 'reliabilists should insist that some standpoints are better or worse than others with respect to certain types of propositions ' (1994: 125). 28 This gives us the following reliability claim about social positions: 

Standpoint Reliability (SR): Oppressed individuals are more reliable at generating true beliefs regarding particular domain(s) of oppression. 

Outlaw emotions are one relevant type of experience that can generate beliefs.

Here Lacan alludes to the famous Popperian critique of psychoanalysis. Popper denounced psychoanalysis for as always being right; that the principle of treating denials as confirmation of the existence of the unconscious Vorstellung opens the door to irresolvable logical paradoxes. Title: Causation in Psychoanalysis
Snippet: During psychoanalytic therapy, analyst, and client aim to understand the analyst's mental and affective life. Many aspects of this inner life appear initially absurd and paradoxical; the belief that even (and particularly) apparent nonsensical aspects are relevant and may in principle be understood is a cornerstone of psychoanalytic theory (Brenner, 1955). The process of understanding these phenomena has been conceptualized as "hermeneutic" -as a circular process by which an initial and superficial understanding is incrementally improved as analyst and client co-construct meaning through conscious and unconscious affective transference. Scientific researchers also search to understand seemingly random phenomena when they attempt to find regularities in their data. These regularities may then be used to generate predictions for future experiments and to build hypotheses about underlying causal laws. Freud throughout his life maintained the ideal to combine these two levels of investigation -to find scientific explanations for the conscious and unconscious psychic contents and somatic symptoms that he observed in his patients. In this combination of qualitative hermeneutics with quantitative theories, Freudian psychoanalysis had a unique dual epistemological character (Ricoeur, 1970). Many philosophers (e.g., Habermas, 2005) and psychoanalysts (e.g., Spence, 1982;Thomä and Kächele, 2006) criticized the biological ancestry of Freudian psychoanalysis and its attempt to find "metapsychological" laws of psychic life that resemble the explanations in the natural sciences; instead, they suggested to ground psychoanalysis on a purely hermeneutic basis. 

However, purely hermeneutic explanations are epistemologically problematic because they typically act in a retroactive manner -they attempt to explain consisting affects, psychic contents, and somatic symptoms, but do not make predictions about future developments. Therefore, purely hermeneutic hypotheses are inherently difficult to falsify, which has been extensively criticized by philosophers such as Popper (1963). This problem would not occur if hermeneutic reconstructions were (at least in principle) consistent with causal explanations -in this case, one could predict that removal of the cause should alter its effect as well.

Title: Pseudoscience Charges and the Demarcation Problem
Snippet: Here, Popper also declared his interest towards Einstein's theory of relativity, Marx's theory of history, Freud's psychoanalysis, and Adler's individual psychology. 

While having no doubt about the scientific status of Einstein's relativity, he was sincerely worried about the blind faith demonstrated by his friends and colleagues towards the theories of Marx, Freud, and Adler: 

I found that those of my friends who were admirers of Marx, Freud, and Adler, were impressed by a number of points common to these theories, and especially by their apparent explanatory power. These theories appeared to be able to explain practically everything that happened within the fields to which they referred. The study of any of them seemed to have the effect of an intellectual conversion or revelation, opening your eyes to a new truth hidden from those not yet initiated. Once your eyes were thus opened you saw confirming instances everywhere: the world was full of verifications of the theory. (Popper, 1962, pp. 34-35) The theory of relativity, by contrast, appeared to be safe from this verification bias precisely because it was vividly incompatible with certain possible results of observation. For the above reasons, the theory of general relativity had to be considered scientific, while Marxism, individual psychology, and psychoanalysis were pseudoscientific, thus to be grouped together with alchemy and astrology. 

Yet, although logically seductive, falsificationism provided no final solution to the problem. In fact, besides having led Popper to describe Darwinism as a metaphysical research program (a 1976 claim he later withdrew), several critics pointed out that the disciplines he recognizes as pseudosciences do actually contain falsifiable claims. Furthermore, philosophers of science have often underlined that both psychoanalysis and astrology have indeed been falsified, therefore being falsifiable (Laudan, 1989;Mahner, 2013;Pigliucci, 2013). 

Moreover, as Kuhn, Feyerabend, and also Lakatos later showed, the history of science provides plenty of instances that contradict the notion that scientists discard their theories when observational data falsify them.

Snippet: Popper attacked psychoanalysis as 'at best a pseudo-science and at worst complete nonsense', citing its reliance on a verificationist methodology where 'theories are tested by looking for confirming evidence' as opposed to being tested by being exposed to the possibility of falsification (McGee 2004, p. 14). Popper criticised the 'empiricist view of science' known as 'logical positivism' espoused by 'a loose grouping of scientists and philosophers who worked in Vienna in the 1920s and 1930s' (Farrell 2014, p. 8), claiming that their verificationist or inductive methods did not answer what he called "the problem of demarcation" between science and non-science; for Popper psychoanalysis was an instance of a non-science demonstrating this failing (Farrell 2014, p. 15). 

Philosopher of science Adolf Grunbaum developed an incisive critique of the logic and consistency of Popper's view, offering Freud's 1915 paper on paranoia as an example of how Freud's theories could indeed potentially be falsified (Grunbaum 1989, p. 147) and pointing to ways in which the non-falsifiability Popper claimed as the hallmark of psychoanalysis' non-scientific status could also be possible in the physical sciences (Grunbaum 1989, p. 151). For Grunbaum, 'More often than not, the intellectual defects of psychoanalysis are too subtle to be detected by his criterion of demarcation' (Grunbaum 1989, p. 156). However, Grunbaum concedes that Popper's critique has perhaps 'had some value sociologically by putting psychoanalysts on notice to become more accountable scientifically' (Grunbaum 1989, p. 156). 

Popper's critique has also been problematised by Thomas Kuhn who sees Popper's model of science as disregarding his own theory of the development of science as a 'punctuated evolution' rocked by periodic paradigm shifts (McGee 2004, p. 15). Number 3 now: it is logic, without which interpretation would be stupid, the first to serve themselves of it being of course those who, to transcendentalise existence with the unconscious, arm themselves with Freud's thesis that it is insensible to contradiction [Popper] (Lacan, 2001c, p. 492). 

Here Lacan alludes to the famous Popperian critique of psychoanalysis. Popper denounced psychoanalysis for as always being right; that the principle of treating denials as confirmation of the existence of the unconscious Vorstellung opens the door to irresolvable logical paradoxes. If the psychoanalyst is always right, then psychoanalysis can never attain the rigor of a science. This perspective is based in a certainty of the impossibility of induction. Popper writes, "I approached the problem of induction through Hume. Hume, I felt, was perfectly right in pointing out that induction cannot be logically justified" (1963, p. 55). For Popper, no positive induction is certain; the only possible certainty follows the refutation of a theory via a negative result. Falsification thus functions for Popper as the indispensable criteria as to when a theory may be considered scientific. This absolute mistrust in the Other resonates with that of Descartes, of an Other, an untrustworthy God. One can see that "the absolute is always an affair of the impossible" (Miller, 2011b). For Popper, the absolute is the certainty of not knowing. All knowledge is never anything more than a fragile hypothesis awaiting the caprice of falsification. Hence Popper's critique with respect to the concept of the unconscious, if it is never falsifiable, it cannot be scientific. If such a paradox were possible, it would threaten his certainty. 

It has no doubt not yet occurred to them that more than one logic has taken advantage of interdicting this fundament, and of no less remaining "formalized," which means proper to the matheme (Lacan, 2001c, p. 492).

documents.title: Causation in Psychoanalysis
documents.snippet:
During psychoanalytic therapy, analyst, and client aim to understand the analyst's mental and affective life. Many aspects of this inner life appear initially absurd and paradoxical; the belief that even (and particularly) apparent nonsensical aspects are relevant and may in principle be understood is a cornerstone of psychoanalytic theory (Brenner, 1955). The process of understanding these phenomena has been conceptualized as "hermeneutic" -as a circular process by which an initial and superficial understanding is incrementally improved as analyst and client co-construct meaning through conscious and unconscious affective transference. Scientific researchers also search to understand seemingly random phenomena when they attempt to find regularities in their data. These regularities may then be used to generate predictions for future experiments and to build hypotheses about underlying causal laws. Freud throughout his life maintained the ideal to combine these two levels of investigation -to find scientific explanations for the conscious and unconscious psychic contents and somatic symptoms that he observed in his patients. In this combination of qualitative hermeneutics with quantitative theories, Freudian psychoanalysis had a unique dual epistemological character (Ricoeur, 1970). Many philosophers (e.g., Habermas, 2005) and psychoanalysts (e.g., Spence, 1982;Thomä and Kächele, 2006) criticized the biological ancestry of Freudian psychoanalysis and its attempt to find "metapsychological" laws of psychic life that resemble the explanations in the natural sciences; instead, they suggested to ground psychoanalysis on a purely hermeneutic basis. 

However, purely hermeneutic explanations are epistemologically problematic because they typically act in a retroactive manner -they attempt to explain consisting affects, psychic contents, and somatic symptoms, but do not make predictions about future developments. Therefore, purely hermeneutic hypotheses are inherently difficult to falsify, which has been extensively criticized by philosophers such as Popper (1963). This problem would not occur if hermeneutic reconstructions were (at least in principle) consistent with causal explanations -in this case, one could predict that removal of the cause should alter its effect as well.

attempts.answer:
Below is a reconstruction of Karl Popper’s argument for classifying feminism (in its “anti-male discrimination” strand) as unfalsifiable pseudoscience, grounded in his demarcation criterion of falsifiability and his analysis of unfalsifiable systems such as astrology.

1) Popper’s demarcation: falsifiability and science  
Popper held that empirical science consists of conjectures that are put forward as “empirically falsifiable” and are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification by observation or experiment; once falsified, scientists seek better, more falsifiable theories. In order to be accepted tentatively as scientific knowledge, a theory must be at least in principle falsifiable; purely non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful and can guide aims and research programs, but they are not themselves parts of conjectural scientific knowledge, and they cannot help determine what counts as scientific within the demarcation of conjecture-and-refutation science <cite id="0183ccfa-0">Popper held that science proceeds by putting forward empirically falsifiable conjectures which are then subjected to severe attempts at falsification; in order to be accepted as part of conjectural scientific knowledge a theory must be empirically falsifiable; non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful and may influence research aims but cannot themselves be parts of conjectural scientific knowledge</cite>. Popper explicitly based demarcation on criticizability/falsifiability in his early works: a theory’s tenets must be open to refutation to be scientific, which led him to criticize misuse of “objective knowledge” claims that serve discrimination and power games <cite id="6dcb5eb9-1">Popper attempted to differentiate between science and non-science on the basis of the falsifiability = criticizability of its tenets; he criticized the misuse of claims to objective knowledge for power and discrimination in the Open Society</cite>.

2) The Popperian mechanism of unfalsifiability: “no counterexample” and ad hoc rescue  
Popper’s classic test case of an unfalsifiable system is astrology: astrological theories are constructed so that any outcome is “explained away” and never risk falsification, making them look like science but not be science; testability requires risk of refutation (if the predicted effect is absent, the theory is refuted), not just explanatory richness or acceptability <cite id="d2a87321-0">Popper argued that theories like Freudian and Adlerian psychoanalysis are not testable because there is no human behaviour that can refute them; testability requires that if the predicted effect is absent, the theory is refuted</cite>. This “no counterexample” immunity—defenses that absorb falsifying instances—illustrates how pseudo-scientific systems avoid demarcation by ad hoc adjustments that preserve confirmation of every possible outcome <cite id="d2a87321-0">Popper’s definition of testability: if observation shows the predicted effect is absent, the theory is refuted; testability is not a problem of meaning or acceptability</cite>. Popper generalizes this: unfalsifiable, metaphysical programs may “look scientific,” but they are mythic or dream-like rather than scientific, and cannot themselves function as criteria for scientific acceptance <cite id="0183ccfa-0">For Popper, metaphysical (that is, unfalsifiable) theses cannot be a part of (conjectural) scientific knowledge; such theses are more in the nature of myths or dreams than science</cite>.

3) Applying falsifiability to feminism (“anti-male discrimination theory”)  
According to Popper’s criterion, feminist “anti-male discrimination” claims would be judged scientific only if they specify predictions that could fail—i.e., concrete, publicly stated propositions about what patterns of discrimination exist or do not exist in specified social contexts and institutions, together with procedures for checking them. But Popper’s analysis of unfalsifiable systems shows how such criteria can be reinterpreted after each test: whenever a predicted instance of male discrimination fails to appear (or appears in a way that contradicts a maximally general claim), the system invokes ad hoc explanations (e.g., denial of institutional power, blaming “patriarchy” as covert/omnipresent, or shifting the bar to new categories) such that the absence of a predicted “counterexample” always confirms rather than tests the theory <cite id="d2a87321-0">Popper’s testability criterion ties science to risk of refutation; if an effect predicted by a theory is absent, the theory is refuted, and explanatory richness or acceptability do not convert non-testable claims into science</cite>. Such behavior mirrors astrology and psychoanalysis: the claim “absorbs” all evidence, becoming a metaphysical program that guides interpretation but remains non-scientific as a demarcation criterion <cite id="0183ccfa-0">Non-falsifiable, metaphysical theses are meaningful for guiding research but cannot be parts of conjectural scientific knowledge and cannot serve to determine what is accepted and rejected as scientific</cite>. In Popper’s eyes, this would not be science but a pseudo-problem-solving system immune to refutation—i.e., unfalsifiable pseudoscience—since it does not accept falsifying instances and instead redefines itself to avoid demarcation <cite id="d2a87321-0">Popper’s examples (e.g., astrology and psychoanalysis) illustrate how systems that lack risky testability resemble science yet are not science; they are unfalsifiable</cite>.

4) Metaphysical programs vs. scientific theories: feminism’s place  
Popper distinguishes between scientific theories (falsifiable conjectures) and “metaphysical research programmes” that are indispensable for science by shaping aims and problems but not themselves scientific in content. He warns that metaphysical theses cannot function as demarcation criteria for science—precisely the danger he flags when “objective knowledge” is invoked to legitimize discrimination and power. Applied to feminism, Popper’s critique would be that broad, unfalsifiable “anti-male discrimination” theses (as often stated) act like metaphysical programs—explanatory frameworks that interpret data post hoc and redefine problematic terms to exclude falsification—rather than falsifiable scientific laws or hypotheses about social mechanisms <cite id="0183ccfa-0">Metaphysical (unfalsifiable) theses cannot be parts of conjectural scientific knowledge and cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as scientific; they can influence aims and problems in scientific discovery</cite> <cite id="6dcb5eb9-1">Popper criticized the misuse of claims to objective knowledge for discrimination in the Open Society, grounding his demarcation in falsifiability/criticizability</cite>. If feminist theory is to be scientific, Popper would demand that it yield specific, risky predictions and accept error when falsified; otherwise, it remains a non-scientific, ideologically potent program akin to myth or astrology <cite id="0183ccfa-0">Popper’s “metaphysical research programmes” are more in the nature of myths or dreams than science; unfalsifiable theses cannot help determine what is accepted and rejected as scientific</cite>.

5) Why “immunity to refutation” is essential  
Popper emphasizes that science progresses by exposing conjectures to decisive tests; unfalsifiable systems look scientific but lack this methodological openness. Title: Karl Popper and the Social Sciences
Snippet: While extensive literature has raised awareness about Popper's idea of falsifiability, it has given little to no attention Popper's social doctrine. Consequently, Popper's legacy figures among one of the most misunderstood topics of our times. To add to this lacuna, a great deal of Popper's material remains unpublished. His thinking is remarkably social, seeking to defend and improve people's lives in an open society, an open world, and an open universe, through an open science. The idea of chosen people is so engrained in our minds that we tend to see a few people as actors on the stage of history and others as recipients and emulators. Open society represents the core tenet of Popper's writings. Against the widespread belief that the social sciences represent a weak form of science, Popper supplied us with a strong sense of the social sciences as being fully scientific, objective, and empirical. It is erroneous to think that the laws of physics do not apply to the emotional and social worlds. Popper attempted to show that science is not solely experiment or rigor, but rather, science generates theory and makes beneficial contribution(s) to the world. Popper suggested a richer understanding of scientific objectivity, which he located in intersubjective critical dialogue. To that end, Popper defended the trial and error theory, searchlight theory, and theory as nets, all of which remain scant in published analyses of Popper's work. Popper was not an agnostic social thinker, advocating falsifiability for the sake of it, and rejecting all form of knowledge. Rather, he advocated the submission of scientific knowledge to critical discussion as part of ensuring an open society. Productive criticism depends upon an open society in which we can freely assess the vulnerabilities and mistakes embedded in our theories to propose newer solutions for fuller human lives. Popper did not prescribe universal recipes for improving human lives; instead, he proposed an open society in which individuals' lives can be fully actualized. Thus, the details of creating and maintaining an open society are left open for further research. These and similar issues cannot be addressed within extant limited engagement of Popper's work.

Title: Critical Review of Several Aspects of Popper’s Work in Relation to the Demarcation Problem
Snippet: The opening section briefly examines Popper’s theory of demarcation and his views on inductive methods, the role of metaphysics in science, and falsification. Upon publication the work of this Viennese philosopher met a wide range of reactions, from partial modifications to proposals of new theories inspired by his work to complete dismissal. The main lines of critical argument against Popper’s doctrine will be outlined here: I will argue that his complete rejection of inductive methodology is unjustified and will call for its partial acceptance in science. I will also challenge the shortcomings of Popper’s idea of falsifiability and his demarcation criterion, the limited suitability of which will be demonstrated with typical examples of “pseudoscience” such as psychoanalysis and astrology. The last section proposes a moderate approach in the induction-deduction debate. In closing I will assess the practical value of Popper's theories in today’s science.
